flashcards.back: The NIST process in SP 800-37 Rev. 2 that integrates security, privacy and supply chain risk management into the system life cycle. It is a repeatable seven-step cycle that ends with an authorization decision and then ongoing monitoring.
flashcards.detail: The RMF is a process, not a control catalog. The catalog is SP 800-53; the RMF tells you when and how to pick, implement, assess and authorize those controls.

flashcards.back: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor. Prepare sets up the organization and system level context; the other six move one system from definition to authorization to ongoing oversight.
flashcards.detail: Prepare was added in Revision 2, so anything that lists only six steps is describing the older revision. Sequence questions love swapping Select and Categorize or Assess and Authorize.

flashcards.back: The step that establishes the context and priorities for managing risk, at both the organization level and the system level. Tasks include assigning risk management roles, setting a risk management strategy, identifying common controls and defining the authorization boundary candidates.
flashcards.detail: Prepare is the only step with tasks at two levels. If a scenario asks what groundwork should exist before a single system is categorized, the answer sits here.

flashcards.back: An organization-wide statement of how it frames, assesses, responds to and monitors risk, including its risk tolerance, acceptable approaches and priorities. It gives system owners and authorizing officials a common basis for decisions.
flashcards.detail: Without an agreed strategy, two authorizing officials will accept very different residual risk for the same system, which is exactly the inconsistency the strategy exists to prevent.

flashcards.back: Risk is managed at Tier 1 (organization), Tier 2 (mission and business processes) and Tier 3 (information systems). Information flows both ways: strategy and tolerance flow down, and system-level results and posture flow up.
flashcards.detail: The RMF itself operates mainly at Tier 3, with Prepare reaching up to Tiers 1 and 2. Expect questions that ask which tier a given activity belongs to.

flashcards.front: Risk management components: frame, assess, respond, monitor
flashcards.back: SP 800-39 describes four components applied at every tier: frame risk (assumptions, constraints, tolerance), assess it, respond to it, and monitor it over time. Together they form a continuous loop rather than a one-time project.
flashcards.detail: Frame comes first because assessment results mean nothing without agreed tolerance and assumptions. A tempting wrong answer starts with assessment.

flashcards.back: The level of risk or degree of uncertainty an organization is willing to accept in pursuit of its mission, as set by senior leaders. Authorizing officials use it to judge whether residual risk is acceptable.
flashcards.detail: Risk tolerance is a leadership decision, not a technical measurement. The ISSO cannot decide it, and neither can the assessor.

flashcards.back: The standard responses are accept, avoid, mitigate, and share or transfer. Mitigation applies controls, avoidance removes the activity, sharing or transferring moves part of the impact to another party such as an insurer, and acceptance knowingly tolerates the residual risk.
flashcards.detail: Buying insurance transfers financial impact, not accountability for protecting the data. Questions often hide this in a scenario about outsourcing.

flashcards.back: Qualitative assessment rates likelihood and impact on descriptive scales such as low, moderate and high. Quantitative assessment uses numeric values such as annualized loss expectancy; semi-quantitative methods map scales to numbers.
flashcards.detail: SP 800-30 allows all three. Qualitative is faster and common for system authorization, while quantitative needs reliable data that many programs lack.

flashcards.back: A function of the likelihood that a threat event occurs and the adverse impact if it does. SP 800-30 builds it from threat sources, threat events, vulnerabilities and predisposing conditions, likelihood and impact.
flashcards.detail: A vulnerability alone is not a risk; with no credible threat or no meaningful impact, the risk can be low. Questions test whether you can tell the ingredients apart.

flashcards.back: A senior official with the authority to formally accept the risk of operating a system and to issue the authorization decision. The AO is accountable for that risk acceptance and cannot delegate the accountability itself.
flashcards.detail: The AO accepts risk; the system owner and ISSO manage it day to day, and the assessor only reports facts. Picking anyone other than the AO for risk acceptance is a classic wrong answer.

flashcards.back: A function (an individual or a group) that provides organization-wide, cross-system risk oversight so that risk decisions are consistent with mission priorities and tolerance. It looks at the portfolio rather than one system.
flashcards.detail: It is a function, not necessarily a job title. Think of it as the body that stops each AO from reasoning about risk in isolation.

flashcards.back: The senior official accountable for the organization's privacy program and for ensuring that privacy requirements and risks are addressed alongside security. In the RMF, privacy controls and plans receive the SAOP's involvement.
flashcards.detail: Privacy is not just a subset of security. When a scenario is about lawful processing of personal data rather than protecting it, the SAOP, not the security officer, owns the answer.

flashcards.back: The official responsible for the procurement, development, integration, modification, operation and maintenance of a system, and for its security and privacy plans. The system owner works with the ISSO and the AO to keep the system authorized.
flashcards.detail: The system owner is accountable for the system as a whole, but does not accept risk on behalf of the organization. That belongs to the AO.

flashcards.back: The individual or group responsible for developing, implementing, assessing and monitoring controls that are inherited by multiple systems, such as a data center's physical security. The provider supplies documentation that inheriting systems rely on.
flashcards.detail: Inherited does not mean ignored. The inheriting system owner still has to confirm the control actually covers their system.

flashcards.back: The information system security officer (ISSO) handles day-to-day security for a specific system; the information system security manager (ISSM) oversees security across a program or site and supervises ISSOs. Titles vary by organization.
flashcards.detail: Both are management and operations roles, not independent assessors. An ISSO who tests their own system's controls does not satisfy assessor independence.

flashcards.back: The individual or team that evaluates whether controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended and producing the desired outcome. The assessor reports findings to the system owner and AO.
flashcards.detail: The assessor reports what is true and does not accept risk or decide authorization. Independence from the system's implementers affects how much the AO can trust the results.

flashcards.back: U.S. law requiring federal agencies to develop, document and implement an organization-wide information security program, using NIST standards such as FIPS 199, FIPS 200 and SP 800-53. The 2014 update modernized the original 2002 act.
flashcards.detail: FISMA is the legal driver; the RMF is how agencies carry it out. Contractors operating federal systems inherit the same obligations by contract.

flashcards.back: The Office of Management and Budget policy on managing federal information as a strategic resource, which directs agencies to use the RMF and to manage security and privacy risk across the life cycle.
flashcards.detail: It is policy that makes NIST guidance operative inside agencies, which is why it appears in governance questions about why a framework is mandatory.

flashcards.back: A voluntary framework organized around six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. Version 2.0 added Govern and widened the audience beyond critical infrastructure.
flashcards.detail: The CSF organizes outcomes for communication and prioritization; the RMF authorizes a specific system. They complement each other rather than compete. CSF 2.0 was released in February 2024 and is a framework, not a control catalog; it is usually mapped to SP 800-53 or ISO/IEC 27001 controls.

flashcards.back: The international standard for an information security management system (ISMS), built on a plan-do-check-act cycle with a risk assessment, risk treatment and a Statement of Applicability. Organizations can be certified by an accredited body.
flashcards.detail: It certifies a management system, not a product or a specific system boundary. The 2022 edition lists 93 controls in four themes in Annex A.

flashcards.back: The ISO guidance for information security risk management, supporting the risk assessment and treatment that ISO/IEC 27001 requires. It describes how to identify, analyze, evaluate and treat information security risk.
flashcards.detail: ISO/IEC 27001 says you must do risk management; ISO/IEC 27005 helps explain how. It is guidance, not a certifiable standard.

flashcards.back: The coordinated management of cybersecurity risks that arise from suppliers, products, services and the paths through which they reach an organization. NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 provides the guidance and the SR control family in SP 800-53 supports it.
flashcards.detail: Supply chain risk is organizational as well as per-system, so expect it in governance questions about vendor oversight and in selection of SR controls.

flashcards.back: A policy states mandatory high-level intent; a standard sets specific mandatory requirements; a procedure lists the steps to carry them out; a guideline offers recommended, non-mandatory advice.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario says employees may deviate "where sensible", it describes a guideline. Mandatory wording signals a policy or standard.

flashcards.back: Protect society, the common good, necessary public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure; act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally; provide diligent and competent service to principals; and advance and protect the profession. The canons are applied in the listed order when they conflict.
flashcards.detail: When two duties collide, the earlier canon wins, so protecting society outranks loyalty to an employer. Ethics questions reward that ordering.

flashcards.back: The set of components and resources that are managed together under the system owner and are covered by one authorization. Everything inside is assessed and authorized as part of the system; things outside are treated as external and handled through interconnections.
flashcards.detail: Boundary mistakes ripple through every later step. A too-large boundary is costly to authorize; a too-small boundary hides risk in components that were left out.

flashcards.back: A specific category of information, such as financial, medical or personnel records, defined by an organization or law, that a system processes, stores or transmits. Each type has its own confidentiality, integrity and availability impact.
flashcards.detail: A system's categorization is built from its information types, so missing one understates the result. SP 800-60 provides the reference lists.

flashcards.back: The federal standard for security categorization of information and information systems. It defines three impact levels (low, moderate, high) for each of confidentiality, integrity and availability.
flashcards.detail: FIPS 199 categorizes; FIPS 200 sets minimum security requirements. They are paired and constantly confused.

flashcards.front: Impact levels: low, moderate and high
flashcards.back: Low means a loss would have a limited adverse effect on operations, assets or individuals; moderate means a serious adverse effect; high means a severe or catastrophic adverse effect.
flashcards.detail: The distinguishing words are limited, serious and severe or catastrophic. Scenarios describe consequences in words and expect you to map them.

flashcards.back: The practice of setting the overall system impact level to the highest value among its confidentiality, integrity and availability impacts, and also the highest across its information types. The result selects the control baseline.
flashcards.detail: One high objective makes the whole system high for baseline purposes, even if the other two are low.

flashcards.back: A system categorization is written as SC system = {(confidentiality, impact), (integrity, impact), (availability, impact)}, for example confidentiality moderate, integrity low, availability low. The overall level used for baselines is the highest.
flashcards.detail: Remember that each objective is rated separately first. Questions give three values and ask for the overall result.

flashcards.back: A two-volume guide for mapping types of information and systems to security categories. Volume 1 describes the process; Volume 2 provides catalogs of information types with provisional impact levels.
flashcards.detail: Provisional levels are starting points. The organization may adjust them with documented justification for its own context.

flashcards.back: The documented purpose, functions, owners, users, information types, components, data flows, environments and interconnections of a system. It is the foundation for categorization and the later plans.
flashcards.detail: In the RMF this is the first task of Categorize. Weak descriptions lead to weak control selection.

flashcards.back: An interconnection security agreement documents the technical and security requirements for connecting two systems; a memorandum of understanding or agreement covers the business and management terms. SP 800-47 gives guidance.
flashcards.detail: The connection partner is outside your boundary, so you cannot assume its controls. The agreement is how you set expectations in writing.

flashcards.back: Recording the system, its boundary, categorization and owners in the organization's inventory so it can be tracked and monitored. Registration is a Prepare-level task in the RMF.
flashcards.detail: A system that is not in the inventory is usually not being monitored, which is itself a risk finding.

flashcards.back: An analysis of how personally identifiable information is collected, used, shared, protected and retained in a system, and of the privacy risks that follow. It is typically triggered by a new system or a significant change to how PII is handled.
flashcards.detail: A PIA is about privacy risk to individuals, not just confidentiality of data. It informs which privacy controls to select.

flashcards.back: Information that can distinguish or trace an individual's identity, alone or combined with other information. The PII confidentiality impact level, discussed in SP 800-122, considers factors such as identifiability, quantity and sensitivity.
flashcards.detail: Information that looks harmless alone can become PII when linked. Exam scenarios often test that linkage.

flashcards.back: A provisional level is the default impact value for an information type from guidance such as SP 800-60. An adjusted level is a documented change made because the organization's specific context, such as volume or mission, justifies a higher or lower value.
flashcards.detail: Adjustments must be justified and approved, and lowering a level should never be done just to reduce the workload of control implementation.

flashcards.back: The catalog of security and privacy controls for systems and organizations. Revision 5 integrates privacy controls into the main catalog, adds the PT and SR families, and states controls as outcomes that apply beyond federal systems. NIST has issued minor releases since publication; Release 5.2.0 (August 2025) added SA-15(13), SA-24 and SI-02(07).
flashcards.detail: Revision 5 moved the baselines out of the catalog into SP 800-53B. Questions about "where do I find the Low, Moderate and High baselines" point to SP 800-53B.

flashcards.back: Controls are grouped into 20 families, each with a two-letter identifier: AC, AT, AU, CA, CM, CP, IA, IR, MA, MP, PE, PL, PM, PS, PT, RA, SA, SC, SI and SR. Revision 5 added PT (PII processing and transparency) and SR (supply chain risk management).
flashcards.detail: Know a handful by function: AC access, AU audit, CM configuration, CP contingency, IA identification and authentication, IR incident response, RA risk assessment, CA assessment and authorization.

flashcards.back: A predefined starting set of controls matched to an impact level: Low, Moderate or High, plus a privacy baseline. The baseline is chosen from the system's security categorization and then tailored.
flashcards.detail: The baseline is a starting point, not a finished answer. Stopping at the baseline without tailoring is a common weak-practice scenario.

flashcards.back: Modifying a baseline so it fits the system and its environment. Tailoring actions include designating common controls, applying scoping considerations, selecting compensating controls, setting parameter values, supplementing the baseline and providing implementation specifics.
flashcards.detail: Tailoring can add or remove, but any removal needs a documented rationale. Dropping controls just because they are inconvenient is not tailoring.

flashcards.back: A reusable set of specifications that tailors a baseline for a particular community, technology, mission or data type, such as a privacy overlay or one for a classified environment. Overlays standardize the tailoring decisions many systems would otherwise make separately.
flashcards.detail: An overlay is applied on top of a baseline, so it is consistent across similar systems. It is often the answer when many systems share the same special needs.

flashcards.back: A control implemented once at the organization or by a provider and inherited by one or more systems, such as physical access to a shared data center. The inheriting system documents which controls it receives.
flashcards.detail: Common controls reduce cost and duplication, but a weak common control weakens every system that inherits it.

flashcards.back: A control in which part is implemented as a common control and part is implemented by the individual system. An example is incident response, where the organization supplies the process and the system supplies system-specific procedures.
flashcards.detail: Both halves must be documented and assessed. Neither the provider nor the system alone covers the whole requirement.

flashcards.back: A control implemented and managed within one system, with the system owner responsible for it. It is not inherited by any other system.
flashcards.detail: The three types, common, hybrid and system-specific, describe who implements the control, not how strong it is.

flashcards.back: An alternative control used when a baseline control cannot be implemented as written, providing a comparable level of protection. It must be justified and assessed like any other control.
flashcards.detail: It compensates for a control that cannot be met; it is not a way to skip assessment. A compensating control that delivers less protection leaves residual risk the AO must accept.

flashcards.back: Tailoring factors that limit where a control applies, for example removing a wireless control from a system that has no wireless capability, or omitting physical controls from a purely virtual component. Each decision is documented.
flashcards.detail: Scoping removes only what does not apply. If the capability exists anywhere in the boundary, the control is still in scope.

flashcards.back: A blank in a control, such as a frequency or a list of events, that the organization fills with a value that matches its risk. Revision 5 formalizes these blanks as organization-defined parameters.
flashcards.detail: A parameter left undefined makes a control untestable. Assessors look for the chosen value before they can judge compliance.

flashcards.back: The standard that defines 17 security-related areas that every federal system must address, and that requires selecting a baseline from SP 800-53 that matches the FIPS 199 impact level.
flashcards.detail: FIPS 199 says how bad a loss is; FIPS 200 says what minimum protection follows. Do not swap them.

flashcards.back: Organization-level controls that support the overall security and privacy program and are not allocated to the Low, Moderate or High baselines. Examples are the program plan and the risk management strategy.
flashcards.detail: They are implemented by the organization, not selected system by system, which makes them a favorite trick when a question asks what appears in a baseline.

flashcards.back: An addition to a base control that adds functionality or strength. Enhancements are written with the base control identifier and a number in parentheses, such as AC-2(1).
flashcards.detail: A baseline may include a base control without its enhancements, or only some of them. Stronger baselines include more enhancements.

flashcards.back: Privacy controls come from the same catalog and are selected with a privacy baseline in SP 800-53B, based on privacy risk rather than impact level alone. They are documented in the privacy plan alongside the security plan.
flashcards.detail: The security baseline does not automatically cover privacy. A system that handles PII needs privacy controls chosen on purpose.

flashcards.back: Recording, in the security and privacy plans, how each selected control will be implemented, who is responsible, and whether it is common, hybrid or system-specific. This is the output of the Select step.
flashcards.detail: Planned in Select, actual in Implement. Questions about "documented but not yet built" test whether you can tell them apart.

flashcards.back: A plan, developed in the Select step, for how the system's controls will be monitored over time: which metrics, how often, who does it, and how results are reported. It conforms to the organization-level strategy.
flashcards.detail: Monitoring is designed early, not bolted on after authorization. Authorization can later depend on this strategy.

flashcards.back: The ISO/IEC 27001 document that lists which Annex A controls apply, whether each is implemented, and why any are excluded. It is a central output of ISO risk treatment.
flashcards.detail: Excluding a control needs justification. The SoA is the ISO counterpart of recording control selection and tailoring decisions in an SSP.

flashcards.back: FedRAMP defines Low, Moderate and High baselines, with a Low Impact SaaS variant, drawn from NIST SP 800-53 for cloud services used by federal agencies. Cloud providers select the baseline matching the data they will host.
flashcards.detail: FedRAMP reuses NIST controls with added cloud-specific requirements, so it does not replace the RMF for the agency.

flashcards.back: A description in the plan of how a control is actually implemented in this system, including mechanisms, responsible roles and any inherited components. It must be specific enough for an assessor to test.
flashcards.detail: Copying the control text is not an implementation statement. A good one says who does what, where and how often.

flashcards.back: The central document describing the system, its boundary, categorization, environment, interconnections and how each selected control is implemented. SP 800-18 gives the traditional format, and Revision 5 treats the security and privacy plans together.
flashcards.detail: The SSP is a living document that is updated on changes, not a one-time deliverable. It is the first item the assessor reads.

flashcards.back: A strategy of layering several independent controls so that a failure of one does not expose the asset. Layers span people, process and technology, such as policy, network segmentation and endpoint protection.
flashcards.detail: Layers must be different in kind. Three copies of the same control are redundancy, not depth.

flashcards.back: Granting users, processes and systems only the access needed for their authorized tasks and for no longer than needed. It limits damage from mistakes, malware and misuse.
flashcards.detail: Least privilege is the standard answer when a scenario shows excessive rights, but it is not the same as separation of duties.

flashcards.back: Dividing a sensitive process among different people so that no single person can complete it alone, such as one person requesting and another approving a change. It reduces fraud and error.
flashcards.detail: Separation of duties splits a task among people; least privilege limits what each person can do. Both are implemented in the AC family.

flashcards.back: An agreed, documented set of settings and components for a system, against which actual configuration is compared and which changes only through formal change control. SP 800-128 provides guidance on security-focused configuration management.
flashcards.detail: Baselines make drift detectable. Without one, you cannot say whether a change was authorized.

flashcards.back: Reducing attack surface by removing unnecessary services, accounts and software and by applying vetted settings, often from published benchmarks or vendor guides. It is done as part of establishing secure configuration baselines.
flashcards.detail: Hardening is an implementation activity done before assessment, so findings about default passwords or open services point back to it.

flashcards.back: Controls the system relies on from a provider are inherited; the system owner remains responsible for the rest. In cloud, providers often publish a customer responsibility matrix that shows which controls are theirs and which belong to the customer.
flashcards.detail: Shared responsibility never means no responsibility. Assessors expect evidence for the customer-side portion.

flashcards.front: Security and privacy awareness and training
flashcards.back: Controls (the AT family) that make users aware of security and privacy risks and train them for their roles, including role-based training for privileged and security staff.
flashcards.detail: Awareness is for everyone; role-based training is for people with specific duties. Training that never reaches privileged users is a common finding.

flashcards.back: Cryptographic modules whose implementation has been validated against FIPS 140 through the Cryptographic Module Validation Program. Federal systems are generally required to use validated modules for protecting sensitive data.
flashcards.detail: Using a strong algorithm is not the same as using a validated module. Expect this in scenarios about federal compliance.

flashcards.back: IA controls establish who or what a user or device is and verify it. Multifactor authentication combines at least two different factor types, such as something you know, have or are.
flashcards.detail: Two passwords are not two factors. Privileged and remote access are the usual places where MFA is required.

flashcards.back: Controls for generating, protecting and reviewing logs that record who did what, so that actions can be traced to individuals and investigated. They include log content, storage capacity, time stamps and protection from tampering.
flashcards.detail: Logging without review or protection fails the purpose. Assessors check that logs are protected and actually looked at.

flashcards.back: Controls for keeping essential functions running or restoring them after disruption, including contingency plans, backups, alternate sites and testing. SP 800-34 guides the planning process.
flashcards.detail: A plan that was never tested is an untested assumption. Business impact analysis sets the recovery priorities.

flashcards.back: Controls for preparing for, detecting, analyzing, containing, eradicating and recovering from security incidents, plus reporting and lessons learned. It is typically a hybrid control with organization-wide process and system-level procedures.
flashcards.detail: Having a plan is not the same as having tested, trained responders. Reporting obligations can be regulatory.

flashcards.back: Controls are administrative, technical or physical in nature, and preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, recovery or compensating in function. A single control, such as a lock or a log review, can be described along both lines.
flashcards.detail: Questions ask for the function in the scenario: stopping it (preventive), spotting it (detective), fixing it (corrective), or discouraging it (deterrent).

flashcards.back: The SR family of controls covers plans, supplier assessments, provenance, component authenticity, notification of supply chain events and disposal. They make supplier risk part of acquisition, implementation and operations.
flashcards.detail: SR controls sit alongside SA acquisition controls. A vendor questionnaire at purchase time is not enough on its own.

flashcards.back: The PT family covers authority to process PII, purposes, consent, notice, data subject access and redress, and limits on use. It was added in Revision 5 to put privacy requirements in the main catalog.
flashcards.detail: PT is about whether and how PII may be processed. The confidentiality of PII is still covered by security families such as AC and SC.

flashcards.back: The engineering discipline, described in NIST SP 800-160, that builds security and resilience into a system through its design and life cycle. It complements control-based compliance with engineering rigor.
flashcards.detail: Compliance asks whether controls exist; engineering asks whether the design makes the system trustworthy. Both feed the Implement step.

flashcards.back: Controls for allocating resources, managing the system development life cycle, acquiring products and services, requiring developer security testing and managing external service providers.
flashcards.detail: SA is where security requirements enter contracts and development. Findings about unsupported software often map here.

flashcards.back: The person or team accountable for operating a specific control and keeping its documentation and evidence current. A control owner can be the system team, the organization or a common control provider.
flashcards.detail: Naming a control owner is part of making the implementation statement testable. A control with no owner usually drifts.

flashcards.back: Records such as configurations, logs, screenshots, tickets and policies that show a control was implemented and is operating. Good evidence is collected as part of normal operations, not only before an assessment.
flashcards.detail: Evidence that exists only at assessment time suggests the control is not truly operating. Assessors prefer recent, system-generated evidence.

flashcards.back: The document that defines the scope, controls, methods, objects, schedule, assessors and rules of engagement for an assessment. It is approved before testing starts so everyone agrees what will be examined and how.
flashcards.detail: The plan comes before the testing and is approved by the system owner or AO. Testing outside the agreed plan is a classic scenario flaw.

flashcards.back: The report that records the assessment results: which controls were satisfied, which were not, the evidence, and the weaknesses discovered. It is one of the main parts of the authorization package.
flashcards.detail: The SAR reports facts and findings. It does not grant authorization and does not decide acceptable risk.

flashcards.back: A document listing each weakness, the resources needed, the responsible person, the milestones and the scheduled completion date for fixing it. It is created from assessment findings and updated until items close.
flashcards.detail: A POA&M is a commitment to fix, not permission to ignore. Items that pass their date without progress are a red flag for the AO.

flashcards.back: The guide for assessing security and privacy controls, supplying assessment procedures that correspond to the controls in SP 800-53 Rev. 5. It is used to build assessment plans.
flashcards.detail: SP 800-53 says what controls exist; SP 800-53A says how to check them. A question that asks how to test an AC control wants 53A.

flashcards.back: Examine reviews documents, configurations and records; interview talks to people; test exercises mechanisms and compares actual behavior with expected behavior. Assessors usually combine methods for stronger evidence.
flashcards.detail: A policy review alone shows intent, not operation. Testing is the strongest method for technical controls.

flashcards.back: The items an assessor looks at: specifications (documents), mechanisms (hardware, software and firmware safeguards), activities (actions people perform) and individuals (people carrying out those activities).
flashcards.detail: Each method fits certain objects, for example you test a mechanism and interview an individual. Questions pair the two.

flashcards.front: Assessment findings (satisfied vs. other than satisfied)
flashcards.back: Each assessment objective is judged as satisfied or other than satisfied, and the reasons are recorded. Other than satisfied findings become weaknesses that feed the POA&M or are remediated.
flashcards.detail: The assessor documents the finding objectively and does not downgrade it to protect the schedule. Severity and residual risk come after.

flashcards.back: The degree to which the assessor is free from influence by those who built or operate the system. The AO decides the level of independence needed, which is higher for higher-impact systems.
flashcards.detail: Independence strengthens the credibility of results. An implementer assessing their own work is a weakness in every scenario that mentions it.

flashcards.back: An agreement that sets the limits of assessment testing: targets, techniques, timing, notification contacts and what must not be touched. It protects both the assessor and the system.
flashcards.detail: A penetration test without written rules can disrupt production or exceed legal authority. Written approval comes first.

flashcards.back: Authorized, simulated attack on a system to find exploitable weaknesses by chaining vulnerabilities as an attacker would. It is a test method that goes beyond scanning.
flashcards.detail: A scan lists potential weaknesses; a penetration test shows whether they can be exploited and what that leads to.

flashcards.back: Automated tools that check systems for known weaknesses, missing patches and insecure settings. Scans support the assessment and continuous monitoring but can produce false positives and miss logic flaws.
flashcards.detail: Scan results need validation. A report full of unverified findings is not an assessment on its own.

flashcards.back: An assessment determines the extent to which controls are effective, often to support a risk decision. An audit is a formal, independent examination against defined criteria, usually to report conformity to a requirement or standard.
flashcards.detail: Both gather evidence; audits emphasize independence and conformance to criteria, assessments feed risk decisions. Many scenarios use the words loosely, so read for purpose.

flashcards.back: An independent organization accredited to assess cloud service providers against FedRAMP requirements. Its assessment results are part of the FedRAMP authorization package.
flashcards.detail: In FedRAMP the independent assessor is a 3PAO. Using an internal team does not meet the independence expected there.

flashcards.back: Examining a representative subset of items, such as accounts or servers, when checking all of them is impractical. The assessment plan documents how the sample was chosen and what the result implies for the whole population.
flashcards.detail: A cherry-picked or tiny sample gives false confidence. The explanation of how it was selected matters as much as the result.

flashcards.back: Fixes made during or immediately after assessment so a weakness can be corrected and reassessed before authorization. Fixed items are noted in the report along with the original finding.
flashcards.detail: Fixing a finding does not erase it from the record. The report still documents what was found and how it was resolved.

flashcards.back: The risk that remains after controls are applied or weaknesses are partially fixed. The AO reviews residual risk before deciding whether to authorize.
flashcards.detail: Zero risk is not an option. The question is whether what is left is within tolerance.

flashcards.back: The extent to which a control is implemented correctly, operating as intended and producing the desired outcome. A control can exist but fail any of these three tests.
flashcards.detail: Implemented is not the same as effective. Scenarios with a deployed tool no one monitors describe an implemented but ineffective control.

flashcards.back: The assessment of privacy controls together with security controls, using the SP 800-53A procedures, with the SAOP involved. It checks that PII is processed as documented and individual rights are supported.
flashcards.detail: Privacy assessment looks at lawful and fair handling, not only protection. A technically secure system can still fail it.

flashcards.front: SOC 2 Type I vs. Type II
flashcards.back: A SOC 2 report is an independent auditor's opinion on a service organization's controls against the trust services criteria. Type I covers the design of controls at a point in time; Type II also tests operating effectiveness over a period.
flashcards.detail: Type II is stronger evidence because it shows controls working over time. A buyer wanting assurance of operation should ask for it.

flashcards.back: An accredited certification body audits the ISMS in two stages, a documentation review and an implementation audit, then performs periodic surveillance audits and recertification. A certificate shows the management system conforms to the standard.
flashcards.detail: Certification covers the scope the organization chose. A narrow scope can make the certificate far less meaningful than it sounds.

flashcards.back: The assessment of controls that come from a provider can rely on the provider's current assessment results and authorization, supplemented by checks of how the customer uses them.
flashcards.detail: Reuse saves effort but must be current. Relying on stale provider results is a gap.

flashcards.back: The set of documents given to the authorizing official: the security and privacy plans, the assessment reports, the POA&M and an executive summary. In practice it is often described as SSP, SAR and POA&M.
flashcards.detail: The AO decides on this package, so incomplete or outdated documents undermine the decision. It is assembled before the decision, not after.

flashcards.back: The step in which the organization analyzes the package and weighs the residual risk against its risk tolerance, to determine the overall risk to operations, assets, individuals and other organizations.
flashcards.detail: Determination comes before the decision. Skipping straight to approval because the schedule demands it is the wrong answer.

flashcards.back: The formal statement by the AO of whether the risk of operating the system is acceptable. It names the decision type, any conditions and the termination date or ongoing authorization.
flashcards.detail: The decision accepts risk; it is not a guarantee of security. Accepting risk is the AO's role alone.

flashcards.back: The decision that the system may operate at acceptable risk, normally for a defined period or under ongoing authorization. It can include conditions the system owner must meet.
flashcards.detail: ATO is the standard approval. The words "operate at acceptable risk" are the key, not "perfectly secure".

flashcards.back: The date on which an authorization expires unless it is renewed or converted to ongoing authorization. It limits how long the risk acceptance stands without new review.
flashcards.detail: An expired authorization means the system should not be operating on that basis. Sequence and scenario questions use dates to test this.

flashcards.back: The AO's decision that the risk of operating is not acceptable, so the system must not operate or must stop operating. It is a legitimate outcome, not a failure of the process.
flashcards.detail: An AO who denies is doing the job correctly. The system can be resubmitted after the weaknesses are addressed.

flashcards.back: A decision by an agency to use a system, service or application that another organization has already authorized, based on reviewing its authorization package. It is common for cloud services.
flashcards.detail: The agency still owns its own risk acceptance, so ATU is a decision, not an automatic inheritance. It saves reassessment work.

flashcards.back: A decision that approves the common controls provided to other systems, so those systems can inherit them. It is separate from the authorization of any one system.
flashcards.detail: If a provider's common controls are not authorized, every inheriting system carries that uncertainty into its own package.

flashcards.back: Requirements the AO attaches to a decision, such as closing certain POA&M items by a given date or limiting how the system is used. Failure to meet them can lead to revoking the authorization.
flashcards.detail: Conditions are enforceable. Treating them as suggestions is a classic mistake in a scenario.

flashcards.back: A deliberate, documented decision to tolerate a risk without further action, made by someone with the authority to do so. Accepted risk is still tracked and revisited.
flashcards.detail: Silence or inaction is not acceptance. Someone with authority has to decide, and the decision must be documented.

flashcards.back: A new authorization decision made after significant changes or when an authorization ends, using updated assessment results. Reauthorization may be a full or targeted effort.
flashcards.detail: Not every change requires full reauthorization; the security impact analysis and organizational policy decide that.

flashcards.back: An approach in which the AO continues to accept risk based on a mature continuous monitoring program rather than periodic reauthorization. The AO reviews up-to-date information on a regular basis and may still set a termination date.
flashcards.detail: It requires a working monitoring program first. Declaring ongoing authorization without one is a false shortcut.

flashcards.back: The U.S. federal program that standardizes security assessment, authorization and continuous monitoring for cloud services, based on NIST SP 800-53 baselines. It promotes the principle of do once, use many times.
flashcards.detail: FedRAMP authorization is reusable evidence, not an agency's own ATU. Each agency still decides whether to use the service. FedRAMP is moving to FedRAMP 20x, which uses automation-based validation and issues certifications in classes; the Rev5 process is being phased out, so the principle of reuse matters more than any one path.

flashcards.back: Compliance means meeting defined requirements; security means actually reducing risk. A system can satisfy a checklist yet remain exposed, or be well protected yet fail documentation requirements.
flashcards.detail: Exam answers that aim only at passing the audit tend to be wrong. The best answer addresses the real risk and the requirement.

flashcards.back: The U.S. law governing how federal agencies handle records about individuals retrieved by personal identifier. Agencies publish a system of records notice (SORN) describing what is collected and why.
flashcards.detail: A SORN is a public notice, not a security control. It is one of the privacy compliance artifacts expected before PII is used.

flashcards.back: Tracing external obligations, such as sector laws, privacy regulations and contract clauses, to the specific controls that satisfy them. One control can meet several requirements.
flashcards.detail: Mapping prevents duplicate work and exposes gaps. When laws conflict, the most restrictive requirement usually drives the control.

flashcards.back: Ongoing awareness of security, vulnerabilities and threats to support risk decisions, as described in NIST SP 800-137. It assesses controls on a defined frequency and reports to decision makers.
flashcards.detail: ISCM replaces the old idea of a one-time assessment every few years. It is ongoing and risk-based, not constant testing of everything.

flashcards.back: SP 800-137 describes defining the strategy, establishing the program, implementing it, analyzing and reporting findings, responding to findings, and reviewing and updating the program. The cycle repeats.
flashcards.detail: The order starts with strategy. Buying tools before defining what to measure is a typical wrong answer.

flashcards.back: How often a control is assessed depends on its volatility, the system impact level, the threat and vulnerability picture, the control's importance, known weaknesses, and the organization's risk tolerance. Not every control needs the same frequency.
flashcards.detail: Higher-impact and more volatile controls are monitored more often. A single schedule for all controls is rarely the best answer.

flashcards.back: The analysis of a proposed change to determine how it affects the system's security and privacy posture before it is made. It is part of change control (CM-4) and supports the decision whether more assessment is needed.
flashcards.detail: It is done before the change, not after. A change that skips analysis is the starting point of many unauthorized-change scenarios.

flashcards.back: A formal process, often with a configuration control board (CCB), for requesting, reviewing, approving, implementing and recording changes. It keeps the baseline accurate and changes traceable.
flashcards.detail: Emergency changes still need review afterward. Undocumented changes make the SSP inaccurate.

flashcards.back: A change likely to affect the system's risk posture enough to need reassessment or reauthorization, such as a new interconnection, a major architecture change or loss of a key control. Organizations define thresholds in policy.
flashcards.detail: Whether a change is significant is a risk judgment, not a count of servers. Examples include moving to a new cloud provider.

flashcards.back: The continuing handling of risk found after authorization, by mitigating, accepting, sharing or avoiding it. Responses are tracked, and the plans and POA&M are updated.
flashcards.detail: Monitoring finds problems; response fixes them. A finding with no owner and date never closes.

flashcards.back: Regular reports to the AO and other leaders on the state of controls, risk and open items, tailored to what they need to decide. The frequency and content follow the monitoring strategy.
flashcards.detail: Reports should be understandable by decision makers. Raw scanner output does not inform a risk decision.

flashcards.back: Quantifiable indicators such as patch latency, open POA&M items or failed log-in attempts that show how controls are performing. Good metrics tie to decisions and can be collected repeatedly, often automatically.
flashcards.detail: A metric no one acts on is noise. Choose measures that connect to risk.

flashcards.back: The structured retirement of a system: notifying stakeholders, removing it from inventory, handling data and media, updating interconnections and keeping records as required. It is the final task of the Monitor step.
flashcards.detail: Forgotten systems keep data and connections alive. Disposal is part of the life cycle, not an afterthought.

flashcards.back: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 (September 2025) describes three sanitization methods, clear, purge and destroy, and treats cryptographic erase as a purge technique for media that encrypt their contents. The method must match the sensitivity of the data and the type of media, and the result should be verified and recorded.
flashcards.detail: Rev. 2 replaced Rev. 1 (December 2014). Formatting or deleting files is not sanitization on its own; destroy is the choice when the media will not be reused or when other methods cannot give enough assurance.

flashcards.back: Keeping the plans, assessment results and POA&M current as controls are reassessed and the system changes. Updates support ongoing authorization and keep the AO's information accurate.
flashcards.detail: An outdated package means the AO is deciding on stale facts. Update after each meaningful change.

flashcards.back: The ongoing process of finding, prioritizing and fixing weaknesses based on risk, with timelines that follow severity and exposure. It is a core part of continuous monitoring.
flashcards.detail: Patching everything at once is not practical; risk-based prioritization is the sound answer, with documented exceptions.

flashcards.back: The gradual divergence of a system from its approved baseline through untracked changes, which can undo hardening and invalidate prior assessment results. Automated comparison and alerts detect it.
flashcards.detail: Drift is why a passed assessment does not stay true. Continuous monitoring exists partly to catch it.

flashcards.back: Continuing review of the controls, performance and incidents of third parties that process the organization's data, using reports, audits, contract terms and notifications. Responsibility for the data stays with the organization.
flashcards.detail: An annual questionnaire is thin oversight. Contract rights to audits and incident notice make oversight real.

flashcards.back: Using incidents, assessment results and monitoring data to improve controls, plans, training and the risk strategy. It closes the loop so the next cycle starts from better information.
flashcards.detail: Skipping lessons learned repeats failures. It is the last step of incident handling and a feeder for ISCM review.

flashcards.back: Governance sets direction, decision rights and accountability. Risk management identifies, assesses, responds to and monitors uncertainty that could affect objectives. Compliance shows that the organization meets its laws, regulations, contracts and own policies. GRC treats the three together so objectives, risk appetite and obligations are aligned instead of managed in separate silos.
flashcards.detail: Compliance is evidence that requirements were met, not proof that risk is low; governance decides how much risk is acceptable in the first place.

flashcards.back: ISACA's framework for the governance and management of enterprise information and technology. It separates governance objectives (evaluate, direct and monitor, or EDM) from management objectives grouped into align, plan and organize (APO), build, acquire and implement (BAI), deliver, service and support (DSS), and monitor, evaluate and assess (MEA).
flashcards.detail: COBIT is not a security control catalog and not a certifiable standard like ISO/IEC 27001; use it to tie IT and security decisions to enterprise goals, and use SP 800-53 or ISO/IEC 27002 for the controls themselves.

flashcards.back: ISO/IEC 27001 sets the requirements for an information security management system, and organizations are certified against it. ISO/IEC 27002 is guidance on controls. The 2022 edition of both groups the controls into four themes (organizational, people, physical and technological) and lists 93 controls, replacing the 114 controls in 14 domains of the 2013 edition.
flashcards.detail: Only ISO/IEC 27001 is certifiable; 27002 is guidance. The Statement of Applicability must be updated to the control set of the edition the organization is certified against.

flashcards.back: The ISO standard that specifies a privacy information management system (PIMS) for organizations that act as controllers or processors of personal data. It is the ISO route to show systematic privacy management and is designed to sit alongside an information security management system.
flashcards.detail: Privacy management is a management system of its own; a certified ISMS does not by itself show that personal data is handled lawfully.

flashcards.front: PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)
flashcards.back: A security standard from the PCI Security Standards Council for any entity that stores, processes or transmits payment card data or can affect its security. The current version is 4.0.1; it has twelve principal requirements in six goals. It is enforced through contracts with card brands and acquiring banks, and is validated by a self-assessment questionnaire or a report on compliance from a qualified assessor.
flashcards.detail: PCI DSS is an industry contractual standard, not a law. Scope is the cardholder data environment, so segmentation, tokenization and outsourcing to a validated provider are common ways to reduce scope.

flashcards.back: The U.S. Department of Defense program for checking that defense contractors protect federal contract information and controlled unclassified information. Level 1 covers 15 basic safeguarding requirements with annual self-assessment. Level 2 covers the 110 requirements of NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 2, assessed by self-assessment or by a certified third-party assessment organization depending on the contract. Level 3 adds selected SP 800-172 requirements and is assessed by the government.
flashcards.detail: The level a contractor needs depends on the type of information in the contract. Level 2 and Level 3 results must be renewed every three years with an annual affirmation of continued compliance (32 CFR Part 170).

flashcards.front: CMMC conditional status and POA&M limits
flashcards.back: A contractor can reach a conditional Level 2 status with open items only if its score is at least 80 percent of the requirements (88 of 110), no open item is worth more than one point (with one narrow exception for non-validated encryption), and the open items are closed and confirmed within 180 days. Level 1 allows no POA&M at all.
flashcards.detail: A POA&M under CMMC is a short-lived path to certification, not a permanent way to carry weaknesses.

flashcards.front: Controlled unclassified information (CUI) and federal contract information (FCI)
flashcards.back: CUI is information the government creates or owns, or that is created for it, that law, regulation or policy says must be safeguarded or have its dissemination controlled. The rules are in 32 CFR Part 2002, including marking, and NIST SP 800-171 protects CUI in nonfederal systems. FCI is information provided by or generated for the government under a contract that is not meant for public release, protected by basic safeguarding rules.
flashcards.detail: CUI is not classified information. Marking is part of the requirement: handlers can only protect what they can recognize.

flashcards.front: HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act)
flashcards.back: U.S. law covering health information held by covered entities and their business associates. The Privacy Rule governs use and disclosure of protected health information, the Security Rule requires administrative, physical and technical safeguards for electronic protected health information, and the Breach Notification Rule requires notice to affected individuals without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery.
flashcards.detail: A business associate agreement is required before a vendor handles protected health information. Larger breaches (more than 500 people in a state or jurisdiction) also require notice to the government and the media.

flashcards.back: The EU General Data Protection Regulation applies to organizations that process personal data while established in the EU, and to organizations anywhere that offer goods or services to people in the EU or monitor their behavior. It sets principles such as lawfulness, purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality, and accountability, and gives individuals rights such as access and erasure.
flashcards.detail: Location of the company does not decide whether GDPR applies; where the people are and what the company does with their data does. A controller decides why and how data is processed; a processor acts on the controller's instructions.

flashcards.back: A controller must notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay and where feasible within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to individuals; a late notice must explain the delay. Individuals must be told without undue delay when the risk is high. The most serious infringements can bring fines up to 20 million euros or 4 percent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.
flashcards.detail: The 72 hours start when the controller becomes aware, not when the investigation ends. Lesser infringements carry fines up to 10 million euros or 2 percent of turnover.

flashcards.back: Executive orders direct federal agencies, and the Office of Management and Budget and NIST turn them into requirements and guidance. Executive Order 14028 on improving the nation's cybersecurity (May 2021), for example, drove federal work on zero trust, software supply chain security and incident reporting. Private organizations feel such orders through contract terms and acquisition rules rather than directly.
flashcards.detail: An executive order does not bind a private company on its own; the obligation arrives as a contract clause, regulation or procurement requirement.

flashcards.back: Requirements come from three kinds of source. Laws and regulations are mandatory and carry penalties (FISMA, HIPAA, GDPR). Contractual requirements bind the parties who signed (PCI DSS through card-brand agreements, CMMC through defense contracts, customer security clauses). Voluntary frameworks and standards are adopted by choice (CSF, COBIT, ISO/IEC 27001 certification).
flashcards.detail: A voluntary framework can become mandatory when a contract or regulator names it, so check the source of each obligation before deciding how strictly it applies.

flashcards.back: A prescriptive framework lists specific requirements every in-scope entity must meet (PCI DSS, CMMC). A risk-based framework has the organization assess risk and then select and justify controls (the NIST RMF, ISO/IEC 27001). Many programs use both: the risk-based process picks controls, and the prescriptive requirements set a floor.
flashcards.detail: Meeting a prescriptive checklist does not show that the organization's own risks are addressed, and a risk-based approach cannot go below a mandatory floor.

flashcards.back: A SOC 2 report evaluates a service organization against up to five trust services categories: security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy. Security (the common criteria) is always included; the others are added according to the services and what customers need.
flashcards.detail: A SOC 2 report is an auditor's attestation, not a certification, and the report states which categories were in scope, so read the scope before relying on it.

flashcards.back: Examples that appear in compliance programs: the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (internal control over financial reporting, which depends on IT general controls), the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (safeguarding customer financial information) and state privacy laws such as the California Consumer Privacy Act. Each has its own scope, so the first compliance task is deciding which apply.
flashcards.detail: Applicability depends on the type of entity, the data and the people affected; one control set can satisfy several laws once the requirements are mapped.

flashcards.back: The FedRAMP modernization announced in March 2025. It replaces document-heavy review with automation-based validation of machine-readable evidence and issues certifications in classes (A, B and C are available; D is planned). FedRAMP has said it will stop accepting new Rev5 certifications on June 11, 2027, so the traditional authorization path is being phased out.
flashcards.detail: The goals are unchanged: do the assessment once, reuse it across agencies, and keep monitoring. The exam concepts of baselines, a 3PAO and continuous monitoring still apply to the traditional path.

flashcards.back: Assurance that a person or system cannot credibly deny having sent a message, approved a transaction or performed an action. It rests on strong identification, digital signatures, trusted time stamps and tamper-resistant audit records, so that evidence ties the action to one identity.
flashcards.detail: Shared accounts destroy non-repudiation. Encryption alone does not provide it, because anyone who holds the key could have created the message.

flashcards.back: Confidentiality protects information from unauthorized disclosure. Privacy is broader: it concerns how personal information about individuals is collected, used, shared, retained and disposed of, and the rights people have over it. A system can keep data confidential and still process it without authority, for an unstated purpose or for too long.
flashcards.detail: Privacy principles usually include notice, consent or choice, purpose specification and use limitation, data minimization, accuracy, security, individual access and correction, and accountability.

flashcards.front: SDLC phases and security in each phase
flashcards.back: Requirements gathering: define security and privacy requirements and the information types. Design: choose the security architecture, model threats and allocate controls. Development: build with secure practices and implement controls. Testing: verify and assess the controls before release. Operations and maintenance: monitor, patch and control change. Disposal: sanitize media, archive records and remove the system.
flashcards.detail: Risk management is applied across the life cycle (SP 800-37 calls the RMF a system life cycle approach). SP 800-64 has been withdrawn; SP 800-160 Vol. 1 is the current NIST engineering reference.

flashcards.back: The stages information passes through for each information type: creation or collection, processing, dissemination, use, storage and disposition. The stages are documented in a data map such as data flow diagrams, entity relationship diagrams, schemas and data dictionaries, so that controls and privacy risks can be tied to where the data actually goes.
flashcards.detail: Different information types in the same system can have different life cycles, retention rules and disposal methods. Backups and test copies are part of the life cycle.

flashcards.back: A diagram of how information moves between people, components, systems and trust boundaries. It is used to confirm the authorization boundary, find interconnections, locate where sensitive data is stored or crosses a boundary, and decide where controls and privacy assessments are needed.
flashcards.detail: An outdated data flow diagram is a common reason for missed information types and unrecorded interconnections; refresh it when the system changes.

flashcards.back: A retention schedule says how long each type of record must be kept to satisfy law, contract and business needs, and when it must be disposed of. Disposal uses verified sanitization or destruction suited to the data and media, and is logged. A legal hold suspends disposal of the affected records until released.
flashcards.detail: Keeping everything forever creates cost and privacy risk and can breach storage limitation rules; deleting too early can breach record-keeping duties. Both are compliance failures.

flashcards.back: Assets are tangible and intangible items of value to the mission. Tangible assets include facilities, people and hardware and networks. Intangible assets include business processes, digital information, firmware, software and services. The system owner identifies and prioritizes assets so that protection effort follows value (RMF task P-10).
flashcards.detail: A hardware and software list is not an asset inventory by itself; people, facilities, services and the information are assets too.

flashcards.front: Security and privacy requirements vs. controls
flashcards.back: Requirements state what the system must achieve or avoid, and come from laws, regulations, policies, contracts and stakeholder needs. They are defined and prioritized, then allocated to the system and its environment. Controls are the safeguards selected and implemented to satisfy those requirements, so each requirement should trace to controls and to assessment evidence.
flashcards.detail: A requirement can be satisfied by different controls; traceability from requirement to control to evidence is what an assessor looks for.

flashcards.front: Other roles: CIO, information owner, mission owner and privacy roles
flashcards.back: The chief information officer oversees information technology and is accountable for the security program, with a senior agency information security officer running it. The information owner or steward has authority over specified information and decides the controls on its handling, retention and disposal. The mission or business owner is accountable for the mission the system supports. Privacy officials, security and privacy architects and systems security engineers support design and requirements.
flashcards.detail: Match the question to the authority: information handling to the information owner, risk acceptance to the authorizing official, day-to-day security to the ISSO.

flashcards.back: The usual sequence is: identify the laws, regulations, contracts and frameworks that apply and the scope; give an executive sponsor and named owners authority; assess the current state with a gap analysis; write and map policies, procedures and controls to the requirements; train and communicate; then test, monitor, report and improve in a repeating cycle.
flashcards.detail: Starting with tools or testing before scope and ownership are agreed is the typical mistake; a program with no accountable owner decays after the first audit.

flashcards.back: A comparison of current practice with the requirements of a framework, law or contract to find controls that are missing, partial or undocumented. The output is a prioritized remediation plan with owners and dates, often tracked in a POA&M or risk register.
flashcards.detail: A gap analysis is a snapshot; it does not replace an assessment or audit, and it must be repeated when requirements change.

flashcards.front: System name, identifier and scope statement
flashcards.back: The system description gives the system a unique name and identifier, an owner, its type and version, the environments it runs in (such as development, test and production), and a scope statement that says what is inside the authorization boundary and what is not. It is the anchor that inventories, plans, assessments and reports all point back to.
flashcards.detail: Two systems with the same name, or a scope statement that never mentions the test environment holding production data, are classic causes of assessments that cover the wrong thing.

flashcards.back: The documented purpose says which missions, business functions and mission or business processes the system supports, who uses it, what it does and what depends on it. Purpose and functions determine which information types the system handles and how severe a loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability would be.
flashcards.detail: Categorization that ignores what the business actually uses the system for will be wrong in either direction; ask the mission or business owner.

flashcards.back: Stakeholders are the people and groups with an interest in the system: the mission or business owner, the system owner, the information owner, users, the authorizing official, privacy and security officials, owners of connected systems and sometimes customers or regulators. Identifying them early shows who must agree on scope, categorization and risk decisions (RMF task P-9).
flashcards.detail: A stakeholder who is found late, such as a partner whose data flows through the system, can force changes to scope and requirements.

flashcards.back: The GDPR requires a controller to carry out a DPIA before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to individuals, for example systematic and extensive profiling with significant effects, large-scale use of special categories of data, or large-scale systematic monitoring of a public area. It describes the processing, assesses necessity and proportionality, assesses risks to individuals and lists measures to address them, and the data protection officer's advice is sought.
flashcards.detail: If a DPIA shows high residual risk that cannot be reduced, the controller must consult the supervisory authority before starting the processing.

flashcards.back: Both analyze privacy risk before a system collects or uses personal data. A PIA is the term used in U.S. federal practice (the E-Government Act requires it for new systems that collect identifiable information). A DPIA is the GDPR legal duty for processing likely to be high risk. A single assessment can often serve both if it covers the content each one requires.
flashcards.detail: The names are not interchangeable on the exam: DPIA signals the GDPR, PIA signals U.S. federal practice, and both are done before processing begins.

flashcards.front: Security objectives for each information type
flashcards.back: For each information type the organization decides how much confidentiality, integrity and availability it needs, using the requirements that apply: federal standards such as FIPS 199, international standards such as ISO/IEC 27001 risk criteria, privacy laws and contractual terms. The result states the objectives per type and is the input to the system impact level.
flashcards.detail: Objectives are set per information type and per objective; a type can need high integrity and low availability, and recording that nuance drives better control selection.

flashcards.back: The organization determines the scope of its information security management system by considering internal and external issues, the requirements of interested parties, and the interfaces and dependencies between its activities and those of other organizations. The scope must be documented, and it sets which locations, services and information the certificate covers.
flashcards.detail: A scope drawn around a single department, while customer data is processed elsewhere, produces a certificate that does not mean what customers think it means.

flashcards.front: Risk impact level under different frameworks
flashcards.back: The U.S. federal approach fixes three impact levels (FIPS 199) that select a baseline. ISO/IEC 27001 has no fixed levels: the organization sets its own risk criteria, assesses risks and selects controls through risk treatment and the Statement of Applicability. The CSF uses organizational profiles and tiers, and the GDPR frames risk as risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals.
flashcards.detail: When a question names a framework, use that framework's own method for deciding how much protection is needed, not the FIPS 199 levels by default.

flashcards.front: PCI DSS scope: the cardholder data environment
flashcards.back: PCI DSS applies to the cardholder data environment: system components that store, process or transmit account data, plus components connected to them or that could affect their security. Segmentation, tokenization and outsourcing to a validated service provider reduce scope. An entity must confirm scope before assessing.
flashcards.detail: Anything on a flat network with the cardholder data environment is in scope, so network design is the main way to shrink the assessment.

flashcards.back: Data classification is an organization policy that labels information (for example public, internal, confidential and restricted) so people know how to handle it. Security categorization under FIPS 199 rates the impact of losing confidentiality, integrity and availability to select a control baseline. The two should be mapped to each other so that labels and baselines agree.
flashcards.detail: Labels drive handling and marking; categorization drives which controls are selected. Neither replaces the other.

flashcards.front: Factors for the PII confidentiality impact level
flashcards.back: SP 800-122 lists factors that raise or lower the harm from exposure of PII: how easily it identifies an individual, the quantity of PII, the sensitivity of the data fields, the context of use, the obligation to protect confidentiality (laws and agreements) and where the PII is stored and who can access it. They are applied in addition to the FIPS 199 confidentiality impact.
flashcards.detail: The same data fields can warrant different levels in different systems; a list of a few hundred names is not the same as a database of millions.

flashcards.back: After the system is categorized, the results are documented in the security, privacy and supply chain risk management plans, must be consistent with the enterprise architecture and the risk management strategy, and are reviewed and approved by senior leaders such as the authorizing official or a designated representative. If not approved, the system owner repeats the categorization and resubmits it.
flashcards.detail: Approval of the categorization comes before control selection starts, because a wrong level selects the wrong baseline.

flashcards.back: The environment of operation is the physical, technical and organizational setting around the system: hosting, networks, shared services it depends on, the people who use it and the rules that apply. Dependencies on shared services are recorded in the system description and handled through inheritance or interconnection agreements.
flashcards.detail: A system that depends on a shared service is only as strong as that service, so record it and confirm what the provider covers.

flashcards.back: The security baseline comes from the system's overall impact level (Low, Moderate or High, from the high-water mark), and a privacy baseline is selected on privacy risk. An organization may start from an organizationally tailored baseline or a Cybersecurity Framework profile instead of the raw SP 800-53B baseline. The choice and its reason are recorded.
flashcards.detail: A baseline is a starting point; picking it is the Select task, and tailoring comes next.

flashcards.back: For each inherited control the plan records which provider supplies it, the provider's current assessment or authorization, what part of the control is covered, and what the customer system must still do. The provider documents the common control; the inheriting system confirms that it fits and attaches the provider's evidence.
flashcards.detail: The statement "inherited from the cloud provider" is not enough; assessors look for the provider, its status and the customer's remaining duties.

flashcards.front: Control enhancements, security practices and mitigating controls
flashcards.back: A control enhancement adds strength or capability to a base control. Security practices are organization-wide habits and standards (for example secure configuration or coding standards) that supplement the controls. A mitigating control reduces a risk when a required control cannot be met in full; it is justified and assessed like any other control.
flashcards.detail: Enhancements are chosen because of the risk to this system. Mitigating controls are chosen because a required control is not possible, and they must offer comparable protection.

flashcards.back: Supplementation adds controls or enhancements beyond the baseline when the system's risk, threat environment, mission or legal obligations call for it, for example stronger protection against a determined adversary or additional privacy controls for sensitive personal data. The risk assessment, not a wish for extra safety, is the justification.
flashcards.detail: Adding controls without a risk reason wastes resources, and refusing to add them when risk requires it leaves the system under-protected.

flashcards.back: Marking labels information, media and output with its classification or handling restrictions so that people and systems apply the right protections. The handling requirements say how each type is stored, transmitted, shared, printed and disposed of. Examples are the banner and category markings for controlled unclassified information, PII and health data handling rules, and the SP 800-53 controls for media marking and security and privacy attributes.
flashcards.detail: Marking and handling rules come from the data's legal and contractual status, so identify them during selection, not after implementation.

flashcards.back: Every tailoring decision is recorded with the control, the action taken (scoping, parameter value, compensating control, supplementation or designation as common), the reason, and the approver. The record lets the authorizing official, the assessor and later maintainers see why the control set differs from the baseline.
flashcards.detail: A removal without a recorded reason looks the same as a mistake, so assessors treat it as a gap.

flashcards.back: Each selected control is designated system-specific, hybrid or common and is allocated to the specific system elements that carry it out: machine elements (hardware, software, firmware), physical elements or human elements. Allocation shows who or what is responsible for each control and where assessment should look.
flashcards.detail: A control that is allocated to nobody is not implemented, whatever the plan says; allocation is where gaps in responsibility show up.

flashcards.back: Owners of common controls, providers, the system owner and other stakeholders agree on who implements and operates each control and what the inheriting system can rely on. Agreements take the form of service level agreements, memoranda, interconnection agreements or inheritance statements, and are reflected in the plans.
flashcards.detail: Without agreement, both parties assume the other covers the control, which is how inherited controls turn out to have no owner.

flashcards.back: Before implementation, the authorizing official or designated representative reviews and approves the security and privacy plans that reflect the selected and tailored controls. Approval confirms that the planned protection is commensurate with risk and gives implementers a fixed target (RMF task S-6).
flashcards.detail: Implementing before the plans are approved risks building the wrong controls and having to redo the work.

flashcards.front: Vulnerability management as part of the compliance strategy
flashcards.back: A continued compliance strategy decides how the system will stay compliant after authorization. Vulnerability management is a core part: scanning frequency, patch timelines by severity, handling of exceptions, tracking of unresolved items in the POA&M, and reporting to stakeholders. It sits beside the continuous monitoring strategy, change control and periodic assessments.
flashcards.detail: The strategy is set during selection so that resources for monitoring are planned with the controls, not added later.

flashcards.front: Control selection under ISO/IEC 27001, PCI DSS and CMMC
