flashcards.back: ISO/IEC 27001 selects controls through risk treatment, from Annex A or other sources, and records inclusions and justified exclusions in the Statement of Applicability. PCI DSS and CMMC set fixed requirements; PCI DSS permits documented compensating controls and, in version 4.0, a customized approach, while CMMC allows only limited, time-bound open items.
flashcards.detail: The more prescriptive the framework, the less room there is to leave a requirement out; the more risk-based, the more the justification matters.

flashcards.front: Organizationally tailored baselines and framework profiles
flashcards.back: An organization can tailor baselines once for its own use, or build a Cybersecurity Framework profile, and make them available to system owners. This is an optional organization-level Prepare task. Systems that start from such a baseline get consistent, pre-approved tailoring and spend less effort selecting controls.
flashcards.detail: Overlays and organizationally tailored baselines both standardize decisions; use the one that matches the question's scope (community of systems or whole organization).

flashcards.back: A plan for how and when the selected controls will be put in place. It sequences work by risk, dependencies and quick wins, estimates the people, tools and funding needed, sets a timeline with milestones, and defines how effectiveness will be judged. It must fit the organization's expectations, the national or international requirements that apply and the privacy and security plans.
flashcards.detail: A strategy is approved before implementation starts; controls that cannot be funded or finished in time are documented as planned implementations, not forgotten.

flashcards.back: Each control needs an estimate of effort, cost and skills, including running costs such as licenses, staff time, monitoring and training, not only the initial purchase. Funding requests are justified by the risk the control reduces. Shortfalls are escalated to the owner who can accept the risk or find resources, and recorded in the POA&M.
flashcards.detail: A control with no owner and no budget will degrade after the first assessment; resourcing is part of implementation, not an afterthought.

flashcards.back: The schedule orders the work so that prerequisites come first, for example identity management before role-based access, logging before monitoring, and network segmentation before restricting flows. Milestones are aligned to the planned assessment and authorization dates, and slips are reported and tracked as planned implementations.
flashcards.detail: Implementing controls out of order can leave them untestable; list the dependencies before committing to dates.

flashcards.front: Control types: management, operational and technical
flashcards.back: The classic NIST grouping describes management controls (policy, planning and risk assessment), operational controls (carried out mainly by people, such as awareness training, physical protection and contingency procedures) and technical controls (carried out by system mechanisms, such as access control, audit logging, authentication and encryption). Common controls are those provided once for many systems.
flashcards.detail: SP 800-53 Rev. 5 no longer assigns controls to these classes, but SP 800-18, older catalogs and the exam outline still use the terms; "common" describes who implements a control, not what kind of control it is.

flashcards.back: Policies, procedures and plans are reviewed and updated at an organization-defined frequency and after defined events such as a significant change, an incident or a change in law. The first control of each SP 800-53 family (such as AC-1) requires a policy, procedures, a named official and this review cycle.
flashcards.detail: The frequency is set by the organization to fit risk, and the event triggers matter as much as the calendar.

flashcards.front: Frequency of security and privacy training
flashcards.back: Literacy training is given to new users and again at an organization-defined frequency, and when system changes or events require it. Role-based training is given before a person gets access or starts the duties and again at the defined frequency. Completion is documented and training records are retained (AT-2, AT-3 and AT-4).
flashcards.detail: Annual refreshers are common practice, but the exam point is that the interval is defined, tracked and evidenced.

flashcards.back: The first control in each SP 800-53 family requires the organization to develop and disseminate a policy and procedures, designate an official to manage them, and review and update them at a defined frequency and after defined events. Policy states intent; procedures give the steps; the other controls in the family implement them.
flashcards.detail: A family whose -1 control has no current policy and procedures is often the first gap an assessor reports.

flashcards.back: A compensating or alternate control is chosen when the specified control cannot be implemented as written. The plan documents why the original is not possible, shows that the alternative gives comparable protection, records the approval by the authorizing official or designated representative, and states a review date or end date. It is assessed like any other control.
flashcards.detail: A compensating control is a justified exception, not a convenience; if the reason goes away, the original control should return.

flashcards.back: A record of identified risks: a description, source, likelihood and impact, owner, chosen response, status and residual risk. It is reviewed regularly, feeds reporting to leaders, and links to the POA&M entries that track remediation. Organizations keep registers at the enterprise level and at the system level.
flashcards.detail: A risk register tracks risks and decisions; a POA&M tracks the work and dates to fix weaknesses. They support each other but are not the same document.

flashcards.front: Documenting planned implementations and residual risk
flashcards.back: When a control cannot be fully implemented by the authorization date, the plan records its status as planned or partial, and the POA&M records the weakness, resources, owner, milestones and dates. The residual risk goes into the risk register so the authorizing official can accept or reject it knowingly.
flashcards.detail: Residual risk that is not documented cannot be accepted properly; it is simply unknown risk.

flashcards.back: Implemented controls are described in the policies, procedures and plans that match the organization's purpose, scope and risk profile. The documents are written for the real system and organization, approved, version-controlled and available to those who use them. Copying generic text that does not describe what is done leaves a gap between paper and practice.
flashcards.detail: Documentation must describe what is actually done; an impressive policy set that no one follows is a finding.

flashcards.back: When the delivered implementation differs from the plan, the changes are documented and the security and privacy plans are updated before assessment (RMF task I-2). The record shows what was built, why it changed and whether the change affects the risk or the control assessment.
flashcards.detail: Assessors test what the plan says; if the plan describes a design that was never built, the control fails for the wrong reason or passes for the wrong one.

flashcards.back: Organizations document and monitor security and privacy awareness and role-based training and retain individual training records for a defined period (AT-4). The records are evidence for audits and show that people received training before access and at the required interval.
flashcards.detail: Training that was delivered but not recorded cannot be shown to an auditor.

flashcards.front: Assessment or audit objectives and scope
flashcards.back: The objectives say what decision the assessment supports, such as an authorization decision, a certification or a customer assurance. The scope names the controls or requirements, systems, locations and period covered. Resources, schedule, deliverables and logistics are written down and agreed with the stakeholders before work starts.
flashcards.detail: Scope that is vague or silently narrowed is the main way an assessment ends up answering a question nobody asked.

flashcards.back: The lead assessor and team, the system owner, control owners, the ISSO, privacy officials, the authorizing official and the points of contact for each area have defined roles. Roles state who provides evidence, who answers questions, who approves the plan and the rules of engagement, who receives results and how disagreements are escalated.
flashcards.detail: The assessor stays independent of those who built or operate the system; the AO sets how much independence is needed.

flashcards.back: Practical arrangements for the assessment: access to facilities, accounts and tools, test windows that avoid critical business periods, backups before intrusive tests, notification of operations and security staff, secure handling of results, work space and communication channels. Logistics are in the plan so testing does not surprise operations.
flashcards.detail: A test run during a month-end close without warning is a logistics failure, even when the technical plan was sound.

flashcards.front: Level of effort: depth and coverage
flashcards.back: Level of effort depends on how many assets and controls are in scope and on the depth (rigor and detail) and coverage (breadth) of the assessment methods. Higher-impact systems and higher-risk controls justify more depth and broader coverage. Assets, methods and sampling are chosen and documented in the plan.
flashcards.detail: More effort is not always better; match depth and coverage to the risk and to the decision the results support.

flashcards.back: Before testing, the assessor reviews what already exists: previous assessment and audit reports, the system security and privacy plans, policies and procedures, the POA&M, architecture and data flow diagrams, and provider reports for inherited controls. A request list tells the system team what to provide, and gaps found here shape the plan.
flashcards.detail: Reusing current prior results saves effort, but stale or out-of-scope results do not give valid assurance.

flashcards.front: Finalizing the assessment or audit plan
flashcards.back: The plan is reviewed by the system owner and other stakeholders and approved by the authorizing official or designated approver. It fixes the objectives, scope, methods and objects, schedule, deliverables, rules of engagement and communication paths. Changes after approval go through the same review.
flashcards.detail: Testing starts only after approval, so that everyone has agreed what will be examined and how.

flashcards.front: Testing methods: penetration testing, control testing and vulnerability scanning
flashcards.back: Testing exercises mechanisms and compares actual behavior with expected behavior. Control testing attempts to use or bypass a control directly, such as signing in with a disabled account. Vulnerability scanning finds known weaknesses broadly and cheaply. Penetration testing validates which weaknesses can be exploited and chained. SP 800-115 groups techniques into review, target identification and analysis, and target vulnerability validation.
flashcards.detail: Choose the technique to match the question: scanning for breadth, control testing for whether a specific control works, penetration testing for exploitability.

flashcards.back: Evidence is checked for being relevant, sufficient, reliable and current. Validation corroborates it with another source: examining a configuration and then testing behavior, re-performing a procedure, observing an activity or comparing logs with records. The integrity of collected evidence is preserved with time stamps, hashes or controlled copies.
flashcards.detail: Evidence from a single self-reported source is weak; corroboration is what turns a statement into assurance.

flashcards.front: Preliminary findings and the initial report
flashcards.back: The initial assessment report records the risks identified, summaries of possible risk mitigation and the preliminary findings. It goes to the system owner to confirm factual accuracy and to start corrective action before the report is final. Because fixes may be made and retested, the final report reflects the situation after that review.
flashcards.detail: Preliminary does not mean unreliable; it means that stakeholders can respond before the results are fixed.

flashcards.back: For each significant finding, a short description of how the risk could be reduced, what it would cost or require and what effect is expected. The summaries help the system owner and the authorizing official compare risk responses without having to design them from scratch.
flashcards.detail: The assessor recommends options; the system owner and authorizing official choose the response.

flashcards.back: Each finding or deficiency receives a risk response: avoid, accept, share, mitigate or transfer. The response is discussed with the stakeholders who will carry it out or bear the risk, assigned to a named owner and documented. Acceptance is made by someone with the authority to accept that level of risk.
flashcards.detail: A response that nobody agreed to carry out is not a response; collaboration and ownership are part of the task.

flashcards.back: When a non-compliant finding is corrected, the control is reassessed to confirm that the fix works and creates no new weakness. The finding records the original result, the correction and the retest result. Items that cannot be fixed in time move to the POA&M.
flashcards.detail: A fix that has not been verified is a claim, not a closure.

flashcards.back: The final report states the result for each requirement or control: compliant, non-compliant or not applicable. Not applicable needs a documented reason, for example that the control addresses a capability the system does not have. A control that was not tested is neither compliant nor not applicable; it is a gap in coverage that the report must explain.
flashcards.detail: In SP 800-53A terms the judgments are satisfied and other than satisfied; other than satisfied also covers cases where the assessor could not get enough evidence.

flashcards.back: Recommendations tie to findings, are prioritized and say what should change and why. The final report is reviewed with the system owner for accuracy, records any disagreement, states scope, methods, limitations and results, and is signed and distributed to the people who will make decisions. It becomes part of the authorization package.
flashcards.detail: Recommendations are advice, not orders; the accountable owner decides what to do with them.

flashcards.back: The plan lists the residual risks and deficiencies after assessment, prioritizes them, assigns owners, and states the resources and time needed to reduce or accept each one. In the RMF it takes concrete form as the plan of action and milestones, which is updated as items close.
flashcards.detail: A response plan without resources and dates is a wish list; the plan is where risk response becomes commitment.

flashcards.back: Risks are ranked by level of risk (likelihood and impact), the value of the affected assets, exploitability, regulatory exposure and the cost and ease of reducing them. High risks and cheap quick fixes are handled first, and the ranking is revisited as new information arrives.
flashcards.detail: Severity ratings from a tool are an input, not the answer; context such as exposure and asset value changes the order.

flashcards.front: Resources and time needed to mitigate
flashcards.back: For each prioritized risk, the plan estimates financial, personnel and technical resources and the elapsed time to mitigate, including dependencies such as vendor patches, change windows and procurement. The estimates set the milestones and completion dates in the POA&M and support funding requests.
flashcards.detail: Dates set without checking dependencies are the usual reason POA&M items slip.

flashcards.back: An internal (first-party) audit is done by the organization on itself. A second-party audit is done by a customer or partner on a supplier. A third-party audit is done by an independent body, such as a certification body or regulator. Independence and credibility rise from first to third party, and each reports against defined criteria.
flashcards.detail: Internal audits prepare for external ones; they do not replace the independence that a certification or regulator demands.

flashcards.back: Audits against a management system standard such as ISO/IEC 27001 classify results as major nonconformities (a requirement not met or a failure of the system), minor nonconformities (an isolated lapse) and observations or opportunities for improvement. Nonconformities require corrective action and verification, and a major one can block certification.
flashcards.detail: Classification affects what happens next: a minor item is corrected on a plan, while a major item can stop the certificate.

flashcards.back: The system owner (or common control provider) assembles the security and privacy plans, the assessment reports, the POA&M and an executive summary, with the supporting evidence, into one version-controlled package. Sensitive content is protected, and the package is submitted to the authorizing official through the agreed channel (RMF task R-1).
flashcards.detail: The package is the authorizing official's only view of the system, so incomplete or inconsistent documents lead to a poor decision or a delay.

flashcards.front: Reviewing the package for completeness and consistency
flashcards.back: Before submission, a review checks that the plans, assessment report and POA&M agree: the same boundary and components, the same categorization, POA&M items traceable to findings, evidence for inherited controls attached, interconnection agreements current and every document dated and approved. Differences are fixed before the AO sees them.
flashcards.detail: A boundary that differs between the plan and the assessment report is a red flag that something was missed or not tested.

flashcards.back: The party who decides compliance depends on the framework: the authorizing official or a designated representative for a federal system, a sponsoring agency or the FedRAMP program office for a cloud service, a certification body for ISO/IEC 27001, an acquirer or card brand for PCI DSS, and a customer or regulator where a contract or law says so. Third-party assessment organizations sit in between, producing the independent assessment.
flashcards.detail: Know whose decision it is before you assemble the documents, because the content and format follow the recipient.

flashcards.back: Criteria that the organization sets in advance, from its risk management strategy, for when a system's risk can be accepted. Examples are no open high-severity weaknesses without a funded plan, limits on how long POA&M items may stay open, and required compensating controls. Clear criteria make decisions consistent across systems and officials.
flashcards.detail: Criteria written after the decision are a justification, not a criterion.

flashcards.back: Residual risk is the risk that remains after controls and planned fixes. The authorizing official considers each remaining weakness and also the combined effect of several of them, including those that share an attack path, risk from inherited controls, interconnected systems and suppliers. The result is compared with the organization's risk tolerance.
flashcards.detail: Several low or moderate weaknesses on the same path can add up to a higher risk than each one suggests alone.

flashcards.back: Before a risk decision, the authorizing official consults the stakeholders affected by it: the system owner, the mission or business owner, the risk executive function, privacy and security officials, common control providers and the owners of connected or inheriting systems. Concurrence shows that they understand and agree to the proposed treatment, but the decision and accountability stay with the AO.
flashcards.detail: A risk that is accepted for your system but lands on someone else's system needs that owner's awareness and agreement.

flashcards.back: Residual risk is recorded in writing in the authorization decision, the POA&M and the risk register, with the risk statement, the rationale for the treatment, conditions, an owner and the date and signatory of the acceptance. The record is retained so that later reviews can see what was accepted and why.
flashcards.detail: A risk accepted verbally in a meeting is not an accepted risk; it is an undocumented one.

flashcards.back: Authorization decisions, significant vulnerabilities and risks are reported to organizational officials such as the risk executive function, the chief information officer and the senior agency official for privacy (RMF task R-5). The reports let leaders see the risk across the portfolio and update the organizational view.
flashcards.detail: Reporting upward is part of the Authorize step, not an afterthought; it feeds the risk management strategy.

flashcards.front: Formal notification of the compliance decision
flashcards.back: The decision is communicated in a signed written notice, such as an authorization decision letter. It states the decision type, the system and boundary, any conditions, the effective date and termination date or ongoing authorization status, and is sent to the system owner, control owners, common control providers, the ISSO and other affected parties. The system registration is updated with the decision.
flashcards.detail: The notice is the record that the system may operate, and under what terms; without it, there is no decision to rely on.

flashcards.front: Sharing the decision with stakeholders and external parties
flashcards.back: Owners of inheriting and interconnected systems, the risk executive function, privacy officials and, where a contract or law requires, customers, regulators or certification bodies receive the decision or the relevant part of it. External statements must match the real scope and status, for example a certificate, an attestation letter or a marketplace listing.
flashcards.detail: Overstating scope, such as advertising a whole service as authorized when only part is, creates legal and trust risk.

flashcards.back: ISO/IEC 27001: a certification body decides and issues the certificate after the audit. PCI DSS: the assessed entity submits an attestation of compliance, supported by a self-assessment questionnaire or an assessor's report on compliance, to its acquirer or card brand. SOC 2: an independent CPA firm issues the report. CMMC: assessment results and affirmations are recorded in the government's systems.
flashcards.detail: The word "authorization" belongs to the federal RMF; other frameworks use certification, attestation or an auditor's opinion.

flashcards.back: Authority to accept risk is assigned by the organization, usually by the level of risk and the system impact, to a named official (the authorizing official for systems, senior leaders for organization-level risk). The acceptance covers a defined scope and period and is reviewed when conditions change.
flashcards.detail: Delegating the work of analysis is allowed; delegating the accountability for accepting the risk is not.

flashcards.front: Weighing a change against risk, operations and compliance
flashcards.back: Before a change is approved, its impact is analyzed on three fronts: the effect on organizational and system risk, on operations (availability, performance, dependencies and support) and on compliance requirements such as baselines, the authorization boundary and mandatory settings. The analysis decides whether the change is routine, needs more assessment or counts as a significant change.
flashcards.detail: A change that looks purely technical can still break a compliance requirement, for example by replacing a validated cryptographic module with one that is not.

flashcards.back: When an approved change alters the approved configuration, the baseline is revised through change control: the new version is recorded, approved and made the reference for comparison and monitoring. The plans and any affected assessment results are updated, and the old baseline is retained for traceability.
flashcards.detail: Changing a system without updating the baseline makes the next comparison show false drift or hides a real one.

flashcards.back: A change request states what is changing and why, the impact analysis, the test results, the rollback plan, the schedule and the approvers. Authorized personnel such as a change control board or technical review board approve it, and the decision is recorded. Approval authority is defined by the risk of the change.
flashcards.detail: A change with no record of who approved it is an unauthorized change, however sensible it was.

flashcards.back: Changes are promoted through environments, usually development, test and then production, and are tested where the environment resembles production. Each deployment has success criteria, a schedule in an agreed window, backups and a rollback (backout) plan that is ready before the change is made.
flashcards.detail: A rollback plan that has never been tried is a hope; rehearse it in the test environment.

flashcards.back: Every change is traceable from request to approval, testing and deployment. Tools compare actual settings with the approved baseline and detect changes without a matching approved record. Unauthorized changes are investigated and reversed or put through the process after the fact, and access to make changes is restricted.
flashcards.detail: A configuration change with no matching ticket is both a compliance finding and a possible security incident.

flashcards.back: An emergency change is made quickly to restore service or stop an exploit, using a faster approval path by a designated emergency approver. It is still documented, tested as far as time allows and reviewed afterward by the normal change body, with any permanent fix going through the regular process.
flashcards.detail: The emergency path is not a way around change control; it moves the paperwork, not the accountability.

flashcards.back: The monitoring strategy sets how often compliance activities are reviewed with stakeholders, for example monthly operational reports, quarterly risk reviews and an annual full review. Frequency follows impact level, volatility, threat and the requirements that apply, and is revisited when conditions change.
flashcards.detail: The right frequency is set by risk and requirement, and then actually kept; a missed review is itself a finding.

flashcards.back: Monitoring covers physical assets (facility access, environmental conditions), logical assets (systems, networks, accounts, configurations and vulnerabilities), personnel (access reviews, joiners, movers and leavers, training status) and change control (changes made versus changes approved). Each area has metrics, owners and reporting.
flashcards.detail: A program that watches only the network misses physical, personnel and change-control risks that appear in the outline.

flashcards.back: The incident response capability is kept ready: plans and contact lists are current, people are trained, and exercises test the process. Incidents are detected, analyzed, contained, eradicated and recovered from, and lessons learned update controls, training and plans. NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (April 2025) aligns incident response with the CSF 2.0 and with overall risk management.
flashcards.detail: Incident response is run as part of risk management, not as a separate emergency function.

flashcards.back: Contingency plans are exercised to find gaps. A tabletop exercise walks through a scenario in discussion, a functional exercise performs parts of the plan in a test setting, and a full exercise or failover test uses real systems. Results are recorded, and the plan, training and recovery procedures are updated (SP 800-34 Rev. 1).
flashcards.detail: An untested plan is an assumption; a plan that was tested once and not after major changes may no longer work.

flashcards.back: Security updates and remediation are applied on risk-based timelines, and each weakness is tracked in the POA&M or ticket system until verified closed. Metrics such as time to remediate and number of overdue items show whether the process works, and exceptions are documented, approved and reviewed.
flashcards.detail: Applying a patch is not the end; verification and recording of closure are what let reports and assessors rely on it.

flashcards.front: Keeping evidence, SLAs and contracts current
flashcards.back: Ongoing compliance needs evidence collected on a schedule (logs, scan reports, access review records, tickets) and documents reviewed and updated: policies, procedures, plans, service level agreements and third-party contracts. Changes in requirements, suppliers or systems trigger updates and are communicated to the stakeholders who rely on them.
flashcards.detail: An SLA or contract that no longer matches how the service is delivered can break compliance without anyone noticing.

flashcards.back: Awareness and training continue after authorization: annual security and privacy awareness for all users, role-based training for privileged and specialist staff, and contingency and incident response training for the people who carry out those plans. Completion is documented and records are retained.
flashcards.detail: Each training type has its own audience and trigger; evidence of completion is as important as the training itself.

flashcards.back: New or changed laws, regulations, contract terms, supplier arrangements, standards versions and threats can change what must be monitored and how often. The monitoring strategy and the mapping of requirements to controls are revised, affected controls are reassessed and stakeholders are told.
flashcards.detail: A monitoring strategy written once and never updated slowly stops matching the obligations it was meant to meet.

flashcards.front: Required testing and vulnerability scanning in audits
flashcards.back: Many requirements set recurring technical testing. PCI DSS, for example, calls for external vulnerability scans by an approved scanning vendor at least quarterly and for penetration testing at least once every 12 months and after significant change. Results are retained as audit evidence, and failures lead to remediation and rescans.
flashcards.detail: Know the cadence your framework requires; a test that is overdue is a finding even if nothing was found when it finally ran.

flashcards.back: Interviews ask the people who actually perform or oversee a control how it works and compare the answers with the documents and evidence. Interviewing operators as well as managers, using consistent questions and keeping notes makes the results usable as evidence.
flashcards.detail: Interview answers show practice and understanding, but they need corroboration with documents or testing.

flashcards.back: After an audit, policies, procedures, plans and the POA&M are updated to reflect findings and corrective actions, and evidence of the corrections is filed for the next audit. Version history shows what changed and why.
flashcards.detail: Fixing the practice but not the document, or the reverse, causes the same finding at the next audit.

flashcards.back: Before retirement, the system owner, mission or business owner, information owner, authorizing official, privacy officials and owners of connected or inheriting systems review the requirements: data retention and legal holds, archive or migration needs, interconnections and shared services, licenses, contracts and notices. The result is a decommissioning plan that everyone has agreed.
flashcards.detail: A system that others depend on cannot simply be switched off; find the dependencies first.

flashcards.back: Retirement follows the plan: users are notified, interconnections are disconnected, accounts, keys and certificates are revoked, the system is removed from monitoring, inventory and network services, data is archived or migrated as required, media is sanitized or destroyed (SP 800-88 Rev. 2), and the system registration and common control inheritance records are updated.
flashcards.detail: Leftover accounts, interconnections and unsanitized media are the usual residual risks of a retired system.

flashcards.back: Records of the decommissioned system are retained for the required period: the final plans and assessment, the decommissioning plan and checklist, disposition and sanitization certificates, the authorization termination notice and approvals. They are shared with the stakeholders who need them, such as the records office, privacy officials and owners of affected systems.
flashcards.detail: The paperwork proves that data was handled properly after the system disappeared.

questions.question: A federal agency is about to start a new system project. Leadership asks what should be in place before the project team begins categorizing the system. Which action belongs to the RMF Prepare step?
options: Select and tailor a control baseline for the system under review
Issue an interim authorization so development can begin
Assign risk management roles and set an organization-wide risk strategy
Prepare the plan of action and milestones for the findings the team expects
questions.explanation: Prepare establishes context at the organization and system level, including roles, the risk management strategy and common control identification. Baseline selection happens in Select, the POA&M is created from assessment findings, and an authorization decision cannot exist before the system is categorized, selected, implemented and assessed.

questions.question: A system owner proposes that the ISSO, who built and operates the system, also decide whether the residual risk is acceptable so the project can launch on time. What is the best response?
options: Approve it as long as the ISSO documents the rationale in the SSP
Approve it, since the ISSO knows the system better than anyone
Have the security control assessor decide, since assessors are independent of the team
Decline; risk acceptance belongs to the authorizing official
questions.explanation: The authorizing official holds the authority and accountability to accept risk on behalf of the organization. Operational knowledge does not confer that authority, documentation does not change who may decide, and the assessor reports the facts but does not accept risk, which would also compromise independence.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the three tiers of risk management in NIST SP 800-39?
options: Mission and business processes sit above the organization level and set its tolerance for risk
Each system sets its own risk strategy, which the organization then rolls up
Strategy and tolerance flow down from the organization, and system results flow back up
The information system tier is informed only by the tiers above it and reports nothing back up
questions.explanation: The tiers are organization, mission and business process, and information system. Direction flows downward, and what is learned at the system level flows upward to inform the other tiers. Systems do not set the strategy, the organization tier is the top, and the exchange is two-way.

questions.question: An organization decides to stop offering a customer feature because protecting the data it requires would cost more than the feature earns. Which risk response is this?
options: Avoidance
Acceptance
Transfer
Mitigation
questions.explanation: Avoidance removes the activity that creates the risk. Mitigation would add controls to keep the feature, transfer would shift some impact to a party such as an insurer while the activity continues, and acceptance would knowingly continue with the exposure.

questions.question: A company buys cyber insurance and signs a contract that makes a hosting provider liable for certain losses. The CIO says the risk is now gone. How should the practitioner respond?
options: Financial impact may be shared, but accountability and residual risk remain
Agree, as long as the insurance premium is lower than the expected annual loss
Disagree, because transfer is not a recognized risk response in any framework
Agree, because transferring risk eliminates the organization's accountability for the data
questions.explanation: Sharing or transferring risk moves part of the financial consequence, not responsibility for protecting the information or complying with obligations. Transfer is a recognized response, and a cheap premium does not remove the accountability or the residual risk.

questions.question: During the first phase of a risk assessment under SP 800-30 the team is establishing assumptions, scope and the risk model. Which component of risk management does this resemble most?
options: Responding to risk
Monitoring risk
Accepting risk
Framing risk
questions.explanation: Framing sets the context, assumptions and constraints that give assessment results meaning. Responding comes after assessing, monitoring follows the response, and acceptance is one possible response, not a stage that sets the basis for assessment.

questions.question: A security officer reports that the organization's file servers have a known vulnerability. No threat actor is known to target the servers, they hold only public data, and they are isolated from other networks. What is the most accurate statement?
options: The risk cannot be determined without a full quantitative analysis
The risk is high because every known vulnerability is a high risk
The risk is likely low since threat and impact are limited
No risk exists at all because the data is public
questions.explanation: Risk combines threat, vulnerability and impact. A vulnerability with little credible threat and a small consequence yields low risk. It is not automatically high, it is not zero because availability and integrity can still matter, and qualitative reasoning is sufficient here.

questions.question: Two agencies assess a nearly identical logistics system. One authorizing official accepts findings that the other would reject outright. Which organizational artifact would best prevent this inconsistency?
options: A shared vulnerability scanner license for all the teams
A documented risk management strategy that states shared tolerance
A longer and more detailed system security plan for each system
An additional assessment report from an outside third party
questions.explanation: The strategy sets common ground for how risk is judged and what level is acceptable. A longer plan documents a system but does not align decisions, tools produce findings rather than tolerance, and another report adds information but still leaves each official free to interpret it differently.

questions.question: A policy states that all laptops must use full-disk encryption. A separate document lists the steps to enable encryption on each laptop model. A third document suggests that users store backups on approved drives. Which pairing is correct?
options: The first is a procedure, the second a standard, and the third a guideline
The first is a guideline, the second a policy, and the third a procedure
The first is a standard, the second a guideline, and the third a policy
The first is a policy, the second a procedure, and the third a guideline
questions.explanation: Policies express mandatory intent, procedures give the steps, and guidelines are recommendations. The other pairings invert the roles, for example by treating the step-by-step document as a guideline or the mandatory statement as optional advice.

questions.question: An organization wants an internationally recognized, certifiable framework for managing information security across the entire enterprise, including documented risk treatment. Which is the best fit?
options: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2
ISO/IEC 27001
FIPS 200
NIST Privacy Framework
questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 27001 specifies an information security management system and offers certification by accredited bodies. The RMF is a process for authorizing systems, the Privacy Framework addresses privacy risk and is voluntary and uncertified, and FIPS 200 sets minimum requirements for federal systems.

questions.question: A practitioner is asked to support a supplier review program. Which NIST publication most directly addresses managing cybersecurity risk from suppliers and products?
questions.explanation: SP 800-161 Rev. 1 covers cybersecurity supply chain risk management. SP 800-88 deals with media sanitization, SP 800-60 maps information types to categories, and SP 800-34 guides contingency planning.

questions.question: In a conflict, a CGRC professional learns that following an employer's instruction would expose the personal data of thousands of customers to harm. Under the ISC2 Code of Ethics, what is the best course?
options: Follow the instruction because duty to the employer always comes first
Follow the instruction but record a written objection some time afterward
Advance the profession by publishing the details of the plan immediately
Protect society and public trust first, declining the instruction and escalating
questions.explanation: The canons are applied in order, and protecting society and public trust ranks above service to principals. Following the instruction ranks the lower duty first, a later objection does not undo the harm, and public disclosure ignores proper escalation and the duty to the employer where possible.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why the RMF is described as risk-based rather than checklist-based?
options: Controls are selected, tailored and accepted based on impact, threat and tolerance
It forbids the use of baselines and requires each control to be hand-selected for every system
It applies the same high baseline to every system to avoid any judgment
It replaces control assessment with attestation by management
questions.explanation: The RMF uses baselines as starting points and then tailors and decides based on risk. It does not forbid baselines, it still requires assessment, and applying a single baseline to everything would be a uniform checklist approach.

questions.question: Which two statements about the authorizing official are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Performs independent testing of the system's technical controls
Is the same person as the security control assessor
Accepts the risk of operating a system on behalf of the organization
Holds the authority to issue an authorization decision
Writes the control implementation statements
questions.explanation: The AO accepts risk and issues the decision. Testing is the assessor's role, implementation statements are written by the system team, and combining the AO with the assessor would undermine independence.

questions.question: Which three options are recognized responses to risk? (Choose three.)
options: Ignore the risk until it materializes
Mitigate the risk by applying controls
Avoid the risk by ending the activity
Deny that the risk exists
Accept the risk with documented authority
questions.explanation: Mitigation, acceptance, avoidance and sharing or transfer are the recognized responses. Ignoring a risk and denying it are not responses; acceptance requires a deliberate, documented decision.

questions.question: Which two documents are produced or maintained as a regular part of an organization-level risk management program rather than for one system only? (Choose two.)
options: A single system's assessment plan
The organization-wide tailored baselines and common control identification
The system's interconnection agreement with one partner
The risk management strategy
The control implementation statements for one application
questions.explanation: Strategy and organization-wide tailoring decisions belong to the organization tier. An interconnection agreement, an assessment plan and implementation statements are specific to a system.

questions.question: The Prepare step in the RMF was introduced in Revision 2 of SP 800-37.
questions.explanation: Prepare was added in Revision 2, which also integrated privacy and supply chain risk management. Earlier revisions began with categorization.

questions.question: The ISSO is the official who formally accepts risk for the system.
questions.explanation: The authorizing official accepts risk. The ISSO manages security for the system day to day and supports the AO with information.

questions.question: A guideline is mandatory in the same way a standard is.
questions.explanation: Guidelines are recommended practices. Standards state mandatory, specific requirements, and policies state mandatory intent.

questions.question: ISO/IEC 27005 provides guidance on information security risk management that supports the risk work required by ISO/IEC 27001.
questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 27005 helps organizations carry out risk assessment and treatment; it is guidance rather than a certifiable standard.

questions.question: Risk tolerance is determined by the security control assessor after testing.
questions.explanation: Risk tolerance is set by senior leadership in the risk management strategy. Assessors report findings against it but do not define it.

questions.question: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 adds a Govern function to the original five functions.
questions.explanation: Version 2.0 added Govern to Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, emphasizing oversight and strategy.

questions.question: A team is defining the authorization boundary for a payroll application. The application depends on a shared identity service run by another business unit with its own system owner. How should the identity service be treated?
options: As out of scope, with no documentation, because another unit runs it
As outside the boundary, documented as an interconnection
As inside the boundary, because the payroll application depends on it heavily
As inside the boundary only during the assessment period
questions.explanation: Components managed under a different owner are generally outside the boundary, but dependencies and connections must be documented and addressed through agreements or inheritance. Including everything that is depended on makes the boundary unmanageable, ignoring it hides risk, and boundaries do not change by phase.

questions.question: A system processes three information types. Their impact ratings for confidentiality, integrity and availability are: type A moderate, low, low; type B low, high, low; type C low, low, moderate. What is the overall system impact level?
options: High
Moderate for confidentiality and low for the rest, so Moderate overall
Moderate
Low
questions.explanation: Following the high-water mark, each objective takes its highest value across types: confidentiality moderate, integrity high, availability moderate. The overall level used for baseline selection is the highest of those, which is high. Averaging or using the most common value understates the integrity impact.

questions.question: A system owner wants to lower an information type's provisional impact from moderate to low to reduce the number of controls. What is required?
options: A new FIPS 199 publication
Only a verbal agreement from the assessor during the briefing
Nothing, because provisional levels are advisory and may be changed freely by the owner
A documented, approved justification
questions.explanation: Provisional levels may be adjusted when documented justification supports it and the process approves it. Convenience is not a valid reason, FIPS 199 is not rewritten per system, and a verbal agreement leaves no record.

questions.question: Which NIST publication provides catalogs of information types with provisional security impact levels to support categorization?
options: FIPS 200
questions.explanation: SP 800-60 maps types of information and systems to security categories. SP 800-53A covers assessment procedures, SP 800-137 covers continuous monitoring, and FIPS 200 sets minimum security requirements.

questions.question: A hospital system holds patient records. A breach of the records would cause severe harm to individuals and lasting damage to the organization. Under FIPS 199 what is the confidentiality impact?
options: Low
Not applicable because the system is not classified
Moderate
High
questions.explanation: A severe or catastrophic adverse effect corresponds to high. Moderate describes serious effects, low describes limited effects, and FIPS 199 applies to all federal information regardless of classification.

questions.question: A new system will connect to a partner's network to exchange files daily. Which document best records the technical and security conditions of the connection?
options: An interconnection security agreement
A contingency plan
A security assessment report
A plan of action and milestones
questions.explanation: The agreement sets the technical and security requirements for connecting two systems. The POA&M tracks weaknesses, the SAR reports assessment results, and the contingency plan covers recovery from disruption.

questions.question: The team notices that a pilot cloud environment contains the same production data as the main system but sits outside the documented boundary. What is the best action?
options: Delete the documentation of the main system to avoid inconsistencies
Leave it undocumented because it is only a pilot environment
Evaluate whether it belongs in the boundary, since it holds the same data
Move it into the boundary but keep its categorization lower than production
questions.explanation: Production data in an environment creates equivalent risk, so the boundary and categorization need to account for it. Calling it a pilot does not change data sensitivity, lowering its categorization ignores the data, and deleting documentation compounds the gap.

questions.question: A privacy officer asks what analysis should be completed when a new application will collect personal data. Which is most appropriate?
options: A business continuity exercise
A penetration test
A privacy impact assessment
A code signing review
questions.explanation: A privacy impact assessment examines how PII is collected, used, shared and retained and the resulting privacy risk. The other options address recovery, technical weakness or software integrity.

questions.question: Which two statements describe correct categorization practice? (Choose two.)
options: Only confidentiality is rated for systems that handle PII
The three values are averaged to produce the overall level
Each of confidentiality, integrity and availability is rated separately
The highest value across them is used for baseline selection
Availability is optional for systems without public users
questions.explanation: FIPS 199 rates all three objectives and the high-water mark governs the baseline. Averaging understates risk, and all three objectives are always considered.

questions.question: Which three items are normally part of a documented system description? (Choose three.)
options: Interconnections with other systems
Personal opinions of the developers
Unverified vendor marketing claims
System purpose and functions
Information types processed
questions.explanation: The description records purpose, information types, components and connections. Opinions and marketing claims are not reliable bases for categorization.

questions.question: FIPS 199 defines three impact levels: low, moderate and high.
questions.explanation: Each of confidentiality, integrity and availability is rated low, moderate or high.

questions.question: The authorization boundary should include every system the application depends on, regardless of who owns it.
questions.explanation: The boundary covers what is managed together under the system owner; dependencies owned by others are addressed through interconnections or inheritance.

questions.question: A PII confidentiality impact level can be considered when determining privacy requirements for a system.
questions.explanation: SP 800-122 describes factors such as identifiability, quantity of PII and sensitivity to determine that level.

questions.question: FIPS 200 is the standard that defines the low, moderate and high impact levels.
questions.explanation: FIPS 199 defines the impact levels. FIPS 200 defines minimum security requirements and ties baseline selection to the impact level.

questions.question: System registration in an inventory helps ensure the system is monitored.
questions.explanation: An unregistered system is easily missed by monitoring, so registration is a Prepare-level task.

questions.question: A system has been categorized as moderate overall. The team asks where to find the starting set of controls for that impact level. Which resource is the best answer?
options: The assessment procedures in SP 800-53A
The categorization tables in SP 800-60
The monitoring guidance in SP 800-137
NIST SP 800-53B control baselines
questions.explanation: SP 800-53B publishes the Low, Moderate and High baselines and the privacy baseline for the catalog in SP 800-53 Rev. 5. SP 800-53A holds assessment procedures, SP 800-60 helps with categorization, and SP 800-137 covers monitoring.

questions.question: A wireless access control is in the Moderate baseline, but the system has no wireless capability anywhere in its boundary. What is the best way to handle the control?
options: Remove it silently because the assessor is unlikely to notice
Implement it anyway to be safe and skip the documentation
Apply a scoping consideration and document the reason
Replace it with a compensating control drawn from a different family
questions.explanation: Scoping is a tailoring action for controls that do not apply, and the rationale must be recorded. Implementing a pointless control wastes effort, silent removal leaves no justification, and a compensating control is for a control that applies but cannot be met as written.

questions.question: A legacy mainframe cannot support the password complexity setting a baseline control requires. Management proposes network isolation, restricted terminals and added monitoring instead. What do these measures represent?
options: Common controls inherited from another system
An overlay applied by the organization
Scoping considerations that remove the requirement entirely
Compensating controls, justified and assessed
questions.explanation: A compensating control provides comparable protection when a required control cannot be met, and it is assessed like any other. The measures are specific to this system rather than inherited, they are not a reusable overlay, and the requirement still applies, so scoping does not remove it.

questions.question: Dozens of systems at an agency handle the same type of sensitive health data and each team keeps re-deciding the same tailoring choices. Which approach is best for consistency?
options: Select the High baseline for every system
Ask each assessor to choose the controls during the assessment
Have each system owner research tailoring on their own each year
Define an overlay for that data type and apply it
questions.explanation: An overlay captures shared tailoring decisions once for a community or data type. Independent research leads to inconsistency, using High everywhere ignores the risk-based approach and costs more, and assessors evaluate controls rather than choosing them.

questions.question: A data center's physical access control is implemented once by the facilities group and used by 25 systems. How should those systems treat it?
options: As an inherited common control, confirming it covers their system
As not applicable because the facilities group handles it
As a hybrid control even though no provider is involved
As a system-specific control that each system must implement separately
questions.explanation: Common controls are implemented once and inherited, and each system documents what it receives and verifies fit. It is not system-specific, it is not hybrid without a split in responsibility, and being handled elsewhere does not make it not applicable.

questions.question: The organization provides an incident response policy and process for all systems, while each system defines its own contacts and system-specific procedures. How is this control best categorized?
options: System-specific
Common
Hybrid
Compensating
questions.explanation: A hybrid control has one part provided at the organization level and another part implemented by the system. If everything came from the organization it would be common, if everything were done by the system it would be system-specific, and compensating describes a substitute, not a split in responsibility.

questions.question: An assessor finds that a baseline control contains a frequency blank, and the system security plan says only "regularly". What is the problem?
options: The parameter is optional and has no effect on how the control is assessed
The control should be removed from the baseline for this system entirely
The control must be treated as a common control from now on
The parameter was never given a value, so the control cannot be tested
questions.explanation: Parameters must be filled in with specific values for the control to be implementable and testable. Removal needs a documented reason, the parameter does not change who implements the control, and an undefined value makes assessment impossible.

questions.question: Which control family was added in SP 800-53 Revision 5 to address the processing of personally identifiable information?
options: PS
PT
PM
MP
questions.explanation: PT, PII processing and transparency, was added in Revision 5. PM is program management, PS is personnel security, and MP is media protection, all of which existed earlier.

questions.question: A reviewer notes that none of the program management controls appear in the Moderate baseline and asks why. What best explains the situation?
options: They are implemented at the organization level and not allocated to baselines
Program management controls are optional for every organization to adopt
Program management controls apply only to systems categorized as High
Program management controls were removed from the catalog in Revision 5
questions.explanation: PM controls support the organization-wide program and are implemented at that level rather than selected per system baseline. They are not optional or restricted to High systems, and Revision 5 retained them.

questions.question: In an ISO/IEC 27001 program, which document lists the applicable Annex A controls, their implementation status and the reasons for any exclusions?
options: The Statement of Applicability
The risk management strategy
The plan of action and milestones
The security assessment report
questions.explanation: The Statement of Applicability records the selection and justification of controls. The assessment report records testing results, the POA&M tracks weaknesses, and the strategy is a high-level organizational statement.

questions.question: A cloud service provider hosting federal data asks which set of baselines it should follow for authorization. Which program defines Low, Moderate and High baselines for cloud services based on NIST SP 800-53?
options: SOC 2 Type II
HITRUST CSF
FedRAMP
PCI DSS v4
questions.explanation: FedRAMP standardizes security authorization of cloud services for federal use. HITRUST and PCI DSS are sector frameworks, and SOC 2 is an audit report, not a federal authorization baseline.

questions.question: Which two actions are recognized tailoring activities? (Choose two.)
options: Skipping the privacy plan for internal systems
Lowering the impact level to shrink the baseline
Selecting a compensating control with justification
Deleting controls that the assessor finds hard to test
Assigning values to organization-defined parameters
questions.explanation: Tailoring includes compensating controls, parameter values, scoping, supplementation and designation of common controls. Changing the baseline to avoid assessment or lowering impact for convenience is not tailoring, and privacy requirements do not disappear for internal systems.

questions.question: Which three items are valid control implementation types? (Choose three.)
options: Advisory
Common
System-specific
Optional
Hybrid
questions.explanation: Controls are common, hybrid or system-specific based on who implements them. Optional and advisory are not implementation types.

questions.question: Which two statements about SP 800-53 Revision 5 are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Privacy controls are integrated into the main control catalog
It replaced SP 800-37 as the authorization process
It contains only controls for federal civilian agencies
It publishes the baselines within the catalog itself
It includes families for PII processing and supply chain risk management
questions.explanation: Revision 5 integrates privacy, adds PT and SR, and moves the baselines to SP 800-53B. It is intended for broad use rather than just agencies, and SP 800-37 remains the process document.

questions.question: Tailoring a baseline requires a documented rationale for removals.
questions.explanation: Decisions must be traceable so the AO and assessor can see why a control was not applied.

questions.question: A hybrid control is implemented entirely by the system owner.
questions.explanation: A hybrid control has a common part and a system-specific part.

questions.question: Overlays are applied on top of baselines to meet the needs of a particular community or technology.
questions.explanation: An overlay standardizes tailoring across similar systems.

questions.question: FIPS 200 specifies the security categories low, moderate and high.
questions.explanation: FIPS 199 does that. FIPS 200 specifies minimum requirements and baseline selection tied to the category.

questions.question: An assessor reviewing the system security plan finds that the statement for a log review control reads, "The organization reviews logs per AU-6." What is the best criticism?
options: It is correct because it cites the control identifier and the family
It repeats the control and does not say who, what, how often or with what tool
It should be shortened so that it mentions only the control number and family
It should be moved out of the SSP and into the contingency plan instead
questions.explanation: An implementation statement must describe how the control is satisfied in this system in testable detail. Citing the control number proves nothing, the content belongs in the SSP, and brevity would worsen the problem.

questions.question: A developer has administrator rights on the production database in order to fix problems quickly, and also approves their own production changes. Which pair of principles is violated?
options: Availability and integrity
Least privilege and separation of duties
Defense in depth and redundancy
Accountability and non-repudiation
questions.explanation: Excess rights violate least privilege, and approving one's own change violates separation of duties. The other pairs describe different ideas; none of them name the two failures in the scenario.

questions.question: A team deploys three firewalls from the same vendor in a row at the network edge and states that this provides defense in depth. What is the best assessment?
options: It is least privilege applied to the network devices and their rules
It is true defense in depth because there are multiple devices at the edge
It is separation of duties applied to the network administration staff
It is redundancy; depth needs different kinds of controls in different layers
questions.explanation: Defense in depth uses diverse layers across people, process and technology so a single weakness does not defeat everything. Repeating the same control is closer to redundancy, and the other principles concern access and task splitting.

questions.question: A cloud provider publishes a matrix listing which controls it implements and which the customer must implement. How should the customer's system owner use it?
options: Use it only as a way to remove controls from the baseline
Treat provider items as inherited and evidence the customer side
Assume the provider is responsible for every control that is listed in it
Ignore it and rely on the provider's published marketing materials
questions.explanation: The matrix defines shared responsibility. The customer must still implement and evidence its portion. Assuming the provider covers everything, relying on marketing or deleting controls all leave gaps.

questions.question: A federal system uses a well-known strong encryption algorithm, but the product is a home-built library. The agency requires validated cryptography. Which statement is correct?
options: Validation can be waived whenever the data stays internal
Replace it with a module validated under FIPS 140
Validation applies only to dedicated hardware devices
Algorithm strength alone is enough to satisfy the requirement
questions.explanation: Federal requirements call for validated cryptographic modules, not just good algorithms. Validation covers software and hardware modules, and it is not waived because data is internal.

questions.question: A security review finds default vendor passwords and unneeded services running on servers. Which implementation activity was most likely skipped?
options: Hardening against a secure baseline
Initial system categorization
Independent control assessment
Authorization package assembly
questions.explanation: Hardening removes defaults and unneeded services as part of implementation. Assessment would discover the problem but does not prevent it, and categorization and packaging are different tasks.

questions.question: The company encrypts its production database but never reviews the logs of who accessed it. Which control family is most clearly weak?
options: Physical and environmental protection
Contingency planning
Audit and accountability
Personnel security
questions.explanation: Without log generation, protection and review, actions cannot be traced to individuals. The other families address recovery, physical safeguards and staff screening.

questions.question: A control is documented as "implemented" because a monitoring tool was purchased, but nobody reviews its alerts. Which description fits best?
options: Implemented but not operating effectively
It is a compensating control for a missing control
It is effective because the tool exists and was paid for
It is a common control provided by the organization
questions.explanation: Effectiveness requires correct implementation, operation as intended and the desired outcome. Owning a tool does not create any of the latter two, and the scenario says nothing of compensation or inheritance.

questions.question: A team finds that a vendor's component was signed with an unknown certificate and the vendor cannot show where it was built. Which control family is the primary home for requirements on provenance and authenticity of components?
options: SR, supply chain risk management
MA, maintenance
AT, awareness and training
PE, physical and environmental protection
questions.explanation: The SR family covers provenance, authenticity and supplier assessment. PE, AT and MA address facilities, training and maintenance.

questions.question: A firewall is a preventive control. A security camera used mainly to record entry is best described as which function?
options: Compensating
Detective
Corrective
Preventive
questions.explanation: Recording events helps identify what happened, which is detective. A preventive control stops the event, a corrective control fixes the effects, and compensating describes a substitute for another control.

questions.question: Someone asks who must supply the evidence that a specific control is operating in the system. Which role is directly accountable?
options: The risk executive
The authorizing official
The senior agency official for privacy
The control owner
questions.explanation: The control owner operates the control and maintains its documentation and evidence. The AO decides on risk, the risk executive oversees across systems, and the SAOP owns the privacy program.

questions.question: The organization's only privacy-related control is that data is encrypted. A privacy officer says that is incomplete. Which implementation area is missing most clearly?
options: Stronger encryption keys on the storage that holds the data
More frequent backups of the data to a second location
Controls on authority, purpose and notice for processing PII
A second firewall placed in front of the database server
questions.explanation: Privacy extends beyond protection to whether and how PII is processed, which the PT family covers. Keys, backups and firewalls are security measures and do not address lawful processing.

questions.question: A system owner says the SSP can be written once before authorization and then archived. Which statement is the best correction?
options: The SSP is owned by the assessor and the system team may not edit it
The SSP is a living document updated as the system changes
The SSP is replaced by the SAR once assessment is finished
The SSP only needs updates when the AO retires or changes roles
questions.explanation: Plans must reflect reality, so changes trigger updates. The AO's retirement is irrelevant, the SAR documents assessment results and does not replace the plan, and the system team maintains the SSP.

questions.question: Which two actions best support defense in depth? (Choose two.)
options: Installing several identical firewalls in sequence
Granting broad access to speed up work
Layering network segmentation, endpoint protection and monitoring
Combining technical controls with policy and training
Relying on a single strong perimeter device
questions.explanation: Defense in depth uses diverse layers of different types. Duplicating one control or relying on one device removes diversity, and broad access undermines least privilege.

questions.question: Which two statements about inherited controls are correct? (Choose two.)
options: The inheriting system never needs evidence
A weakness in a common control can affect every inheriting system
Inherited controls are always system-specific
The system owner must still understand and document what is inherited
Inheritance removes the need to assess anything
questions.explanation: Inherited controls reduce effort but not accountability, and their weakness propagates. Inheritance does not remove assessment or evidence, and inherited controls are by definition not system-specific.

questions.question: Which three are examples of evidence an assessor might request to confirm implementation? (Choose three.)
options: Verbal assurances only
System configuration exports
Marketing brochures
Change tickets with approvals
Log samples showing reviews
questions.explanation: Configurations, logs and tickets show that controls exist and operate. Verbal statements alone and marketing materials are weak, unverifiable evidence.

questions.question: Separation of duties and least privilege describe the same principle.
questions.explanation: Separation of duties splits a task among people, while least privilege limits each person's access to what is needed.

questions.question: Using a strong algorithm automatically means the cryptography is FIPS validated.
questions.explanation: Validation applies to the module that implements the algorithm, not only the algorithm.

questions.question: The customer remains responsible for its portion of controls when using a cloud provider.
questions.explanation: Shared responsibility divides, not removes, accountability.

questions.question: A detective control is intended to stop an event from occurring.
questions.explanation: Detective controls identify events; preventive controls stop them.

questions.question: Role-based training is intended only for people with no security duties.
questions.explanation: It is aimed at people with specific security responsibilities, such as administrators.

questions.question: The security and privacy plans are normally updated after significant changes to the system.
questions.explanation: Plans must stay accurate so assessment and authorization rely on current facts.

questions.question: An assessor is about to start testing a production system. Which document should be agreed and approved first?
options: The security assessment report from the last cycle
The plan of action and milestones
The authorization decision letter
The security assessment plan with rules of engagement
questions.explanation: The plan defines scope, methods, schedule and rules, and must be approved before testing so everyone agrees what will happen. The POA&M and SAR are created from results, and an authorization decision comes after assessment.

questions.question: An assessor wants to confirm that a firewall rule set matches what the SSP says. Which assessment method most directly checks actual behavior of the mechanism?
options: Examine the SSP only
Interview
Review of the organization's policy
Test
questions.explanation: Testing exercises the mechanism and compares actual behavior to expected behavior. Interviews reveal what people say, and reading the SSP or policy shows intent, not what the device actually does.

questions.question: An assessor reviews an access control policy and finds it well written. Staff say they follow it, but nobody has checked the accounts. What is the best next step?
options: Mark the control other than satisfied because policies cannot be evidence
Skip the control because it is administrative
Mark the control satisfied because the policy and staff statements agree
Examine or test the real account configurations
questions.explanation: Documents and interviews show intent and perception; operation needs evidence from the system. Marking it satisfied is premature, marking it failed without checking is unfair, and administrative controls are still assessed.

questions.question: During an assessment, the system owner fixes a misconfiguration the assessor found, and the assessor retests it successfully. How should the report reflect this?
options: Remove the finding from the report because it was already fixed
Convert the fixed finding into a formally accepted risk
Record the finding along with the remediation and retest
Leave the finding open until the next scheduled assessment occurs
questions.explanation: The report is a record of what was found and what was done. Deleting it hides history, leaving it open ignores the retest, and risk acceptance is not needed for a resolved weakness.

questions.question: An AO wants stronger confidence for a high-impact system. Which assessment choice best increases credibility of the results?
options: Reduce the number of controls assessed to save time
Use assessors independent of the developers and operators
Have the ISSO assess the controls they personally implemented and operate
Rely only on self-attestation signed by the system owner
questions.explanation: Independence reduces bias and increases trust, particularly for higher-impact systems. Self-assessment and attestation lack independence, and fewer controls reduce coverage.

questions.question: A tester wants to run an exploit against a payment server during business hours. The rules of engagement do not mention the server. What should the tester do?
options: Stop and obtain written approval before proceeding
Proceed because the system is generally in scope for the program
Run it on a similar test system and report the result as production
Proceed with the test but notify the owner afterward
questions.explanation: Testing must stay within the agreed rules, and changes need approval. Proceeding without it risks disruption and legal exposure, notice afterward is too late, and misreporting test results is dishonest.

questions.question: A vulnerability scan reports hundreds of critical findings. Several are in software that the system does not use. What is the best action?
options: Accept the risk of all of them without review
Validate findings and remove false positives
Report all of them because the tool rated them critical
Ignore all scan findings because scanners are unreliable
questions.explanation: Scan results require validation to separate real weaknesses from false positives. Blind reporting wastes effort, ignoring findings leaves true weaknesses, and accepting risk requires analysis.

questions.question: An assessment finds weaknesses that cannot be fixed before the planned authorization date. What should the organization create to track the fixes?
options: A new security categorization
A new risk management strategy
A plan of action and milestones
A revised system boundary
questions.explanation: The POA&M lists the weaknesses, resources, owners, milestones and dates. The strategy and categorization are not changed by findings, and changing the boundary to hide weaknesses is improper.

questions.question: A cloud provider hosts a federal system and is assessed against FedRAMP requirements. Which party performs the independent assessment?
options: The software vendor's sales engineer
The cloud provider's development team
A third-party assessment organization
The agency's help desk
questions.explanation: The 3PAO provides independent assessment for FedRAMP. The provider's own team lacks independence, and the others are not assessors.

questions.question: A customer wants evidence that a service provider's controls operated effectively across the previous nine months. Which report is most appropriate?
options: A SOC 2 Type I report
A vendor-written security whitepaper
A SOC 2 Type II report
A list of the provider's policies
questions.explanation: Type II tests operating effectiveness over a period. Type I covers design at a point in time, and whitepapers and policy lists do not provide independent evidence of operation.

questions.question: The assessor documents that a backup control was implemented but the restores were never tested, so the desired outcome was never confirmed. Which aspect of control effectiveness is missing?
options: Categorization of the system
Independence of the assessor
Producing the desired outcome
Implementation of the control at all
questions.explanation: Effectiveness means correct implementation, operation as intended and producing the desired outcome. Backups exist, so implementation is present; untested restores leave the outcome unproven. The other options are unrelated to the gap.

questions.question: A privacy officer asks whether the assessment will cover whether PII is used only for stated purposes. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Only encryption of the PII is within the scope for this assessment step
Privacy is assessed only by external privacy auditors, never by the team
Privacy is outside the scope of the RMF assessment step entirely
Privacy controls are assessed with security controls, including PII use
questions.explanation: Privacy controls are assessed together with security controls, including purpose limitation and notice. Limiting scope to encryption misses PT-type controls, and privacy is part of the RMF.

questions.question: Which two methods are standard assessment methods in SP 800-53A? (Choose two.)
options: Presume
Interview
Examine
Delegate
Estimate
