questions.question: Which three belong in the preparation for an assessment or audit? (Choose three.)
options: Establishing stakeholder roles and responsibilities
Outlining objectives, scope, schedule and deliverables
Issuing the final authorization decision
Reviewing previous assessments and system documentation
Closing all POA&M items
questions.explanation: Preparation sets roles, scope, schedule and deliverables and reviews existing evidence. The authorization decision and POA&M closure come after testing and reporting.

questions.question: Which two statements about the final assessment report are correct? (Choose two.)
options: It is approved by the assessor alone with no review for accuracy
It omits findings that management has already agreed to fix
It states each result as compliant, non-compliant or not applicable with reasons
It records recommendations tied to findings and any disagreement from management
questions.explanation: The final report records results, justified not-applicable decisions, recommendations and disagreements. It does not hide fixed findings, and it is reviewed with the system owner for factual accuracy.

questions.question: Which two items does a risk response plan normally contain? (Choose two.)
options: A promise to accept every risk without review
Resources and time required to mitigate each risk
The assessor's personal opinion of the system owner
Prioritized residual risks and deficiencies with owners
questions.explanation: The plan turns findings into commitments with priorities, owners, resources and time. Opinions of individuals and blanket acceptance are not part of it.

questions.question: Which three are SP 800-115 technique groups for security testing and assessment? (Choose three.)
options: Target vulnerability validation
Target identification and analysis
Review techniques
Authorization decision techniques
Contract negotiation techniques
questions.explanation: SP 800-115 groups techniques into review, target identification and analysis, and target vulnerability validation. The other two are not groups in that guide.

questions.question: Corrective actions for non-compliant findings are reassessed and validated before the finding is closed.
questions.explanation: Reassessment confirms the fix works and introduces no new weakness; otherwise the closure is only a claim.

questions.question: A control that was not tested in an assessment can be reported as not applicable without any explanation.
questions.explanation: Not applicable needs a documented reason. An untested control is a coverage gap to be explained.

questions.question: A second-party audit is performed by a customer or partner on its supplier.
questions.explanation: Second-party audits sit between internal (first-party) audits and independent third-party audits.

questions.question: A finding of other than satisfied can mean the assessor could not obtain enough information to decide.
questions.explanation: SP 800-53A says other than satisfied covers anomalies in implementation or operation and also cases where evidence is insufficient, with the reasons given in the report.

questions.question: Assessment recommendations are binding orders that the assessor can enforce.
questions.explanation: Recommendations advise the system owner and authorizing official, who decide the response.

questions.question: The SSP lists twelve components in the boundary, but the assessment report covers only nine. What should happen before the package goes to the authorizing official?
options: Delete three components from the SSP so that the documents agree
Submit as is and let the AO decide whether the difference matters
Ask the assessor to rename the nine components so the count matches
Reconcile the documents and assess or explain the three components
questions.explanation: The package must be consistent, and untested components are a coverage gap that must be assessed or explained. Deleting components hides them, and renaming does not change what was tested. Submitting the mismatch pushes the problem to the decision maker.

questions.question: A federal system owner has finished and reviewed the authorization package for a new system. To whom is it submitted for the authorization decision?
options: The authorizing official or a designated representative
The security control assessor who performed the assessment
The ISSO who wrote the system security plan
The vendor that supplied the system software
questions.explanation: The package supports the authorizing official's risk decision. The assessor already produced the assessment, the ISSO helped write the plan, and the vendor has no authority over the decision.

questions.question: Two authorizing officials in the same agency accept very different open weaknesses on similar systems. What would most directly make future decisions consistent?
options: A rule that each AO must write a longer explanation after deciding
Documented acceptance criteria from the risk strategy, set in advance
A shared mailbox where the AOs can talk about their decisions afterward
A requirement that assessors also vote on every decision
questions.explanation: Criteria set in advance, such as limits on severity and age of open items, give officials a common basis. Longer explanations and discussion after the fact do not change the standard, and assessors do not decide risk.

questions.question: The assessment shows ten moderate weaknesses, all on the same internet-facing subsystem and chainable into one attack path. How should the authorizing official judge the risk?
options: Consider the combined effect of the weaknesses, not each one alone
Treat the overall risk as moderate because every single item is moderate
Ignore the weaknesses because none is rated high
Treat each as independent and accept them one by one
questions.explanation: Aggregate residual risk considers weaknesses that combine or share a path, which can exceed the rating of any single item. Judging items alone understates risk.

questions.question: An authorizing official plans to accept a risk that, if realized, would also affect a partner agency connected to the system. What is the best practice?
options: Accept the risk without telling the partner so that no delays arise
Inform the partner's owner and get concurrence before accepting
Ask the partner to accept the risk on the official's behalf
Ask the assessor to make the decision for both agencies
questions.explanation: Risk treatment that affects other organizations needs their awareness and agreement, while the accountable official still decides. Hiding it, shifting the decision or asking an assessor are all inappropriate.

questions.question: An authorizing official says in a meeting that the remaining risk is acceptable but nothing is written down. What should the team do?
options: Treat the spoken statement as sufficient and file the meeting notes
Record the statement in the risk register only and skip the decision letter
Have it recorded in writing with rationale, conditions, owner and date
Wait for the next assessment to decide whether it was accepted
questions.explanation: Acceptance must be documented formally, signed by an authorized official, with rationale and conditions. Informal notes or leaving it open do not create a record anyone can rely on.

questions.question: After an authorization decision, which parties should receive formal notification in addition to the system owner?
options: Only the security control assessor, who needs the decision to file the final report
Only the vendor, so that it can update its product roadmap and release plans
Common control providers, inheriting system owners and risk oversight officials
No one, because the decision is an internal matter for the AO to keep private
questions.explanation: Decisions and significant risks are communicated to the people who depend on the system or oversee risk. Limiting notification to the assessor or vendor, or to no one, leaves those parties unaware of the conditions.

questions.question: In an ISO/IEC 27001 program, who issues the certificate once the audit is complete?
options: ISO itself, after reviewing the audit report
The organization's top management, by self-declaration
The certification body, after it reviews the audit results
The auditing team's lead auditor alone, with no further review
questions.explanation: Certification bodies, accredited to do so, make the certification decision and issue the certificate. ISO writes the standard and does not certify, and self-declaration is not certification.

questions.question: A merchant has completed its PCI DSS self-assessment questionnaire. What does it normally provide to its acquirer to show compliance?
options: A SOC 2 Type II report from its hosting provider for the same period
An ISO/IEC 27001 Statement of Applicability for the whole company
An authorization to operate issued by its own department manager
An attestation of compliance supported by the questionnaire
questions.explanation: PCI DSS compliance is shown with an attestation of compliance backed by the questionnaire or an assessor's report. A SOC 2 report, a Statement of Applicability and an internal ATO are different instruments.

questions.question: A contractor completes a CMMC Level 2 self-assessment. Where must the results and affirmation be submitted?
options: To the card brands through the merchant's acquiring bank
To the supervisory authority within seventy-two hours of the assessment
To the HHS Office for Civil Rights through its public breach portal
Into the Department of Defense's Supplier Performance Risk System
questions.explanation: CMMC results and affirmations are recorded in the DoD systems, including SPRS. Card brands, GDPR supervisory authorities and the HHS Office for Civil Rights belong to PCI DSS, GDPR and HIPAA.

questions.question: A sales brochure says the company's entire platform is authorized, but only one module completed the authorization. What is the best response?
options: Leave it, since the remaining modules will probably be authorized
Add a footnote in small print and keep the headline unchanged
Remove the authorized module from the brochure instead
Correct the statement to match the authorized scope and status
questions.explanation: External statements must reflect the real scope and status; overstating compliance creates legal and trust risk. A footnote or hoping for later approval does not fix a misleading claim.

questions.question: Which three checks belong in the review of an authorization package before submission? (Choose three.)
options: Evidence for inherited controls is attached and current
The documents are written in the same font and layout
The package has no executive summary
The boundary and components match across the documents
POA&M items trace back to assessment findings
questions.explanation: Consistency of the boundary, traceability of the POA&M and current evidence for inherited controls make the package reliable. Formatting is cosmetic and an executive summary is part of the package.

questions.question: Which two items belong in the formal notification of an authorization decision? (Choose two.)
options: The private notes of the assessor about the system owner
The names of employees who failed security training
The decision type and any conditions
The effective date and the termination date or ongoing authorization status
A promise that the system has no remaining weaknesses
questions.explanation: The notice states the decision, conditions and dates. Personal notes, a guarantee of no weaknesses and unrelated staff information do not belong.

questions.question: Which two statements about residual risk documentation are correct? (Choose two.)
options: It is recorded only in the assessor's private notes
It is recorded in writing with rationale, conditions and the accepting official
It is kept in the authorization decision, POA&M and risk register
It is unnecessary when every weakness has a compensating control
questions.explanation: Formal documentation names the accepting official and the rationale and is kept in the records leaders and assessors use. Compensating controls reduce risk but residual risk is still recorded.

questions.question: Several low-rated weaknesses can combine into a risk that is higher than any single item suggests.
questions.explanation: Aggregate risk considers shared attack paths and dependencies, so the combined effect can exceed the individual ratings.

questions.question: When stakeholders concur with a risk treatment, they take over the authorizing official's accountability for it.
questions.explanation: Concurrence shows agreement and awareness, but the accountable official still decides and remains responsible.

questions.question: A SOC 2 report is issued by the service organization about its own controls.
questions.explanation: The report is an opinion written by an independent CPA firm; the service organization supplies a description and assertion.

questions.question: An authorization decision should be communicated in a formal written notice that states conditions and dates.
questions.explanation: The signed notice is the record of the decision and its terms.

questions.question: Acceptance criteria for risk are best defined after the authorizing official has made the decision.
questions.explanation: Criteria set in advance give consistent decisions; criteria invented afterward only justify what was already decided.

questions.question: A team proposes upgrading a database engine. The upgrade replaces the cryptographic module with one that has not been validated, and a compliance requirement calls for validated cryptography. What is the best action?
options: Approve it because the new module offers noticeably better performance
Approve it and then update the compliance requirement afterward to match
Approve it because database engine upgrades are always routine changes
Analyze risk and compliance impact and do not approve it as proposed
questions.explanation: Change analysis weighs risk, operational effect and compliance requirements. A change that breaks a mandatory requirement is not approved as proposed. Performance and routine labels do not change the requirement.

questions.question: A developer pushes a configuration change straight to production and files a ticket the next morning. What is the most accurate description?
options: A normal change, since the ticket was eventually created the next day
An unauthorized change to investigate and bring through the process
An approved change, because developers may approve their own work
An emergency change, because it was made outside working hours
questions.explanation: Changes need approval by authorized personnel before deployment. A ticket after the fact does not make a change authorized, self-approval defeats separation of duties, and a true emergency uses a defined expedited path.

questions.question: A change request has an approved schedule and test results but no rollback plan, and the maintenance window is tomorrow night. What should the change board do?
options: Approve it because the test results look good and the schedule is set
Approve it and ask operations to improvise a rollback if needed
Hold approval until a rollback plan and success criteria exist
Cancel all future changes until a rollback policy is written
questions.explanation: A rollback plan is part of deploying safely. Good tests do not replace it, improvising during failure is risky, and canceling all changes is out of proportion.

questions.question: A team has only ever tested changes directly in production because the test environment is "out of date". What is the best improvement?
options: Continue testing directly in production but only do it after working hours
Keep a production-like test environment and promote changes through it
Remove the test environment altogether to avoid any further confusion
Test only those changes that the product vendor flags as being risky
questions.explanation: Changes are validated in an environment like production before deployment. Testing in production after hours still risks the live service, removing the test environment worsens the problem, and vendor flags alone are not a test strategy.

questions.question: Configuration monitoring reports several changes on a server with no matching approved change records. What is the best response?
options: Ignore them because monitoring tools often produce so many false alerts
Approve them all in one bulk request so that the change records match
Treat them as possible unauthorized changes and investigate them first
Disable the monitoring rule that produced the alerts to cut the noise
questions.explanation: Changes without matching records are both a compliance gap and a possible security event, so they are investigated and then reversed or processed through change control. Ignoring, bulk-approving or disabling the rule hides the problem.

questions.question: An exploit is being used against a public service late on Saturday, and the fix cannot wait for the weekly change board. What should happen?
options: Wait until the regular change board meets again on Monday morning
Apply the fix without keeping any record, to avoid extra paperwork
Let the first available engineer decide alone and keep no record of it at all
Use the emergency path with designated approval, then review it later
questions.explanation: Emergency procedures give a faster approval route with accountability and a later review. Waiting leaves the exploit open, and making unrecorded changes or leaving it to anyone defeats control.

questions.question: A monitoring plan checks network devices and servers but says nothing about facility access, staff access reviews or unapproved changes. What is the best assessment?
options: It omits physical assets, personnel and change control
It is complete, because only logical assets can be monitored
It is too broad, because monitoring should cover one device type only
It is correct, because personnel are monitored only by the HR department
questions.explanation: Ongoing monitoring covers physical and logical assets, personnel and change control. The statement that only logical assets can be monitored is false, and personnel monitoring is part of the security program, not left to HR alone.

questions.question: The contingency plan for a system was last exercised three years ago, and since then the system moved to a new data center. What is the best step?
options: Leave the plan alone, since it passed the original test years ago
Exercise the plan in the new environment, record results and update it
Archive the plan and rely on the new hosting provider's own plan instead
Rewrite the plan to be shorter and simpler without ever testing it
questions.explanation: Significant changes require the plan to be exercised again so gaps are found. A past passing result, handing over the responsibility or shortening the plan without testing leaves the assumption unverified.

questions.question: A new state law adds a requirement for annual encryption verification for systems like yours. What is the best response?
options: Wait for the next scheduled audit before looking at the new law and its scope
Update the mapping and monitoring strategy, reassess controls, inform stakeholders
Assume existing controls already comply and make no changes to documents or testing
Ask the vendor to update its marketing materials about encryption in its products
questions.explanation: Changes in legal requirements feed back into the monitoring strategy and mapping, with reassessment of affected controls and communication to stakeholders. Waiting, assuming compliance or changing marketing leaves the obligation unmet.

questions.question: A hosting provider announces new subprocessors that will handle the organization's data. Which action best supports ongoing compliance?
options: Accept the change because suppliers are entitled to change without notice at all
Ask the provider to withdraw its notice so that the records stay unchanged
Record the change only in the provider's own internal documents and portals
Review it against requirements and update the contract, SLA and risk records
questions.explanation: Supplier changes can alter risk and obligations, so the organization reviews them and updates its contracts, SLAs and risk records. Accepting silently or leaving the record with the provider loses oversight.

questions.question: A merchant asks which recurring technical tests PCI DSS expects for its external systems. Which pair is closest to the requirement?
options: Quarterly external scans by an approved vendor, annual penetration testing
Vulnerability scans every five years and no penetration testing at any time
Penetration testing every month and no vulnerability scans of any kind at all
Only a yearly review of written policies with no technical testing of any kind
questions.explanation: PCI DSS expects quarterly external scans by an approved scanning vendor and penetration testing at least every 12 months and after significant change. The other options set intervals or omit tests that the standard requires.

questions.question: During an audit of access control, the auditor interviews only the IT director. What is the best improvement?
options: Interview several more directors and rely on their summaries of daily practice
Replace all interviews with a review of the written policy and nothing else
Ask the IT director to answer on behalf of the whole team and sign it off
Also interview the administrators who operate the control and corroborate
questions.explanation: Interviews are most useful with the people who operate the control, and the answers are corroborated with documents and tests. Directors' summaries, policy review alone and proxy answers show intent, not practice.

questions.question: A server is shut down for retirement, but its interconnection to a partner and several service accounts remain active. What was missed?
options: Raising the impact level of the retired system before it is switched off
Writing a brand new system security plan and privacy plan for the retired system
Disconnecting interconnections and revoking access when removing the system
Authorizing the retired system for ongoing operation by the authorizing official
questions.explanation: Removal from operation includes disconnecting interconnections, revoking access and updating inventories. Raising the level, writing a new plan or reauthorizing do not belong to retirement.

questions.question: Data from a system scheduled for retirement is subject to a legal hold. What should the decommissioning plan do?
options: Sanitize the media on schedule because the retirement date was set
Move the data to a personal laptop for convenience
Delete the data after copying only the summary report
Preserve the data in an approved archive while the hold applies
questions.explanation: Legal holds override normal disposal. The plan archives the data and records the decision. Scheduled sanitization or deleting the data destroys material that must be kept.

questions.question: Who should review the requirements for decommissioning a payroll system before it is shut down?
options: The system owner, information owner, mission owner, AO and dependent system owners
Only the help desk manager, because it receives all the questions about the payroll system
Only the vendor, because it supplied the payroll software and knows how it works
Only the independent security assessor, who reviewed the system in the last assessment cycle
questions.explanation: Retirement affects data retention, dependent systems and approvals, so the accountable stakeholders review the requirements together. A single group such as the help desk, vendor or assessor cannot cover them.

questions.question: Which three belong in a change request record? (Choose three.)
options: The personal opinions of staff about the change
The approvals by authorized personnel
The authorization termination date of the system
The rollback plan and success criteria
The impact analysis on risk, operations and compliance
questions.explanation: A change record shows the impact analysis, rollback and success criteria and approvals. The termination date and personal opinions do not describe the change.

questions.question: Which two are covered by ongoing monitoring of a system and its assets? (Choose two.)
options: Only the marketing performance of the product
Changes made compared with changes approved
Only the color and layout of the user interface
Only the vendor's sales figures
Physical access to facilities that house the system
questions.explanation: Monitoring covers physical and logical assets, personnel and change control. Interface layout, marketing performance and vendor sales are not control-related.

questions.question: Which three should be retained and shared with stakeholders after decommissioning? (Choose three.)
options: The decommissioning plan and checklist
Active administrator passwords for the retired system
The decommissioned system's live network access
The authorization termination notice
Certificates showing media sanitization or destruction
questions.explanation: Records of the retirement, data disposition and termination are retained as evidence. Active credentials and live access should have been revoked, not kept.

questions.question: Which two statements about contingency plan exercises are correct? (Choose two.)
options: A tabletop exercise walks through a scenario in discussion
A single successful test is valid regardless of later changes
Results are recorded and used to update the plan and training
Exercises are unnecessary when a plan is stored securely
questions.explanation: Exercises range from discussion to full failover, and results drive updates. A past test does not cover later changes, and storing a plan securely does not show it works.

questions.question: An emergency change may skip documentation permanently because speed matters most.
questions.explanation: The emergency path speeds up approval, but the change is still recorded and reviewed afterward, and permanent fixes go through the regular process.

questions.question: A change may be deployed directly to production without testing as long as a rollback plan exists.
questions.explanation: A rollback plan limits damage but does not replace testing in an environment that resembles production.

questions.question: Training records for incident response and contingency training should be retained as evidence.
questions.explanation: Completion records show that people were trained at the required times and are requested during audits.

questions.question: Revisions to an approved baseline are made through change control and recorded.
questions.explanation: Baseline changes are approved and versioned so that comparison and monitoring use the correct reference.

questions.question: Documentation of a decommissioned system is destroyed immediately because the system no longer exists.
questions.explanation: Records are retained for the required period and shared with stakeholders as evidence of proper disposal and for legal and audit needs.

lessons.title: Governance, Risk Strategy and the RMF
lessons.summary: How organizations govern security and privacy, frame risk, assign roles and use the NIST Risk Management Framework to run the whole life cycle.
lessons.reading:
Governance is how an organization decides who may make decisions about security and privacy risk, using what rules, and who is held accountable. Management then carries those decisions out. A CGRC professional works in the space between the two: turning leadership's appetite for risk into repeatable steps that individual systems follow. The framework that does this for U.S. federal systems, and that many other organizations copy, is the NIST Risk Management Framework described in SP 800-37 Revision 2.

The RMF has seven steps: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize and Monitor. Prepare is the one people forget, because it happens before any individual system is in front of you. At the organization level it assigns risk management roles, sets a risk management strategy that states risk tolerance, and identifies controls that can be shared across systems. At the system level it identifies the mission the system supports, the stakeholders, the information it will handle, and a first idea of the authorization boundary. Skipping Prepare is the root cause of many later problems, such as two officials accepting very different amounts of risk for similar systems.

SP 800-39 explains where risk decisions live. Tier 1 is the organization, which sets strategy and tolerance. Tier 2 is mission and business processes, where leaders decide which processes matter and how much security they need. Tier 3 is the individual information system, where the RMF steps are carried out. Direction flows down and results flow up. At every tier the same four activities repeat: frame the risk, assess it, respond to it and monitor it. Framing comes first because an assessment is meaningless without agreed assumptions, constraints and tolerance.

Roles matter because the exam asks who may do what. The authorizing official accepts risk and issues the authorization decision. The risk executive function looks across systems so decisions stay consistent. The system owner manages the system and its plans, the information system security officer supports daily security work, the control owner operates a particular control, the common control provider supplies inherited controls, and the security control assessor evaluates the controls independently. The senior agency official for privacy owns the privacy program. No one else can accept risk in the AO's place, and the assessor does not decide on authorization.

Around the RMF sit other authorities. FISMA and OMB Circular A-130 make the RMF mandatory for federal agencies. The NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 organizes outcomes for communication around its six functions, including the new Govern function. ISO/IEC 27001 provides a certifiable management system, with ISO/IEC 27005 offering risk guidance. Supply chain risk, covered in SP 800-161, is part of governance because suppliers affect every system. When two duties conflict, the ISC2 Code of Ethics tells you to protect society and the public trust first.

The outline asks for more than the RMF vocabulary, so tie these ideas into the same picture. Governance, risk management and compliance (GRC) are three views of one job: leaders decide direction and risk appetite, risk management finds and treats the uncertainty, and compliance shows that obligations were met. Compliance evidence is not proof that risk is low, so a program reports both. Frameworks such as COBIT separate board-level governance (evaluate, direct, monitor) from management activity, while the RMF, ISO/IEC 27001 and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework supply the risk and control structure.

A system is protected through its whole life, which is why the SDLC matters to a CGRC professional. Requirements gathering defines security and privacy requirements and the information types, design allocates controls and models threats, development builds and implements them, testing verifies them, operations and maintenance keep them working through monitoring, patching and change control, and disposal sanitizes media and keeps the required records. In the same way each information type has a life cycle of creation or collection, processing, dissemination, use, storage and disposition. Documenting it in a data map shows where data flows, where retention rules apply and when disposal is due, and a legal hold can suspend disposal.

The core security properties are confidentiality, integrity, availability and non-repudiation, which gives proof of origin through signatures, time stamps and tamper-resistant records, plus privacy, which concerns the lawful, limited and transparent handling of personal information and not only its secrecy. Assets include people, facilities, services and information as well as hardware and software. Requirements come from laws, contracts and policy; they are defined, prioritized and allocated to the system, and controls are selected to satisfy them. Roles beyond the core RMF set include the chief information officer, the information owner or steward (who decides how information is handled, kept and disposed of), the mission or business owner, and privacy officials. A new compliance program starts with the obligations and scope, an accountable owner and a gap analysis, and then runs as a repeating cycle of mapping, training, testing and reporting.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to governance and risk? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a city. The council decides how much risk the city will tolerate and writes the building code, which is governance. Individual builders then follow the code for each building, which is management. The RMF is the inspection process that every building passes through: the plans are reviewed, the construction is inspected, a chief inspector signs off on occupancy, and later inspections make sure nothing has been changed unsafely. The chief inspector, like the authorizing official, is the only person who may sign off, and a builder cannot sign off on their own work.
commonTraps: Prepare is a step of the RMF in Revision 2; older material that lists six steps describes the previous revision.
The authorizing official accepts risk; neither the ISSO nor the assessor can do so, however well they know the system.
Transferring or sharing risk with an insurer or supplier does not remove the organization's accountability for protecting the data.
The RMF is a process; SP 800-53 is the control catalog and SP 800-53B holds the baselines. Do not swap them.
Privacy is not the same as confidentiality; a confidential system can still process personal data without authority or for too long.
Compliance program work starts with obligations, scope and an accountable owner, not with tools or testing.
lessons.scenario: An agency has three business units building similar systems. Each has an authorizing official, and each has made different judgments about acceptable risk, so one unit's approved system would not be approved in another. The CISO proposes a risk management strategy that states shared tolerance, a common set of tailored baselines and a risk executive function that reviews exceptions. The CIO objects that it adds meetings. The CISO points out that inconsistent decisions have already cost months of rework when systems were moved between units.
lessons.onTheJob: In real programs, the hardest part of governance is getting leaders to state their risk tolerance in concrete terms. People who say they have low tolerance for risk often approve exceptions under schedule pressure. Write tolerance as thresholds and decision rights, for example which findings an AO may accept alone and which go to the risk executive. When you are asked for the best answer on an exam, favor the one that follows the defined roles and the documented strategy, because that is how a real program stays defensible when something goes wrong.

lessons.title: Compliance Frameworks, Laws and Contracts
lessons.summary: Telling legal, contractual and voluntary requirements apart, and knowing the main frameworks and laws a CGRC professional meets: ISO/IEC 27001, PCI DSS, CMMC, HIPAA, GDPR, FedRAMP and executive orders.
lessons.reading:
Every compliance requirement has a source, and the source tells you how strict it is and who enforces it. Laws and regulations are mandatory and carry penalties: FISMA for federal agencies, HIPAA for health information, the GDPR for personal data of people in the EU. Contractual requirements bind the parties who signed: PCI DSS reaches merchants through their agreements with acquiring banks and card brands, CMMC reaches defense contractors through contract clauses, and customers add their own security terms. Voluntary frameworks such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, COBIT and ISO/IEC 27001 certification are adopted by choice until a law or contract names them. Executive orders direct federal agencies, and their effect on a private company arrives through acquisition rules and contracts.

Frameworks also differ in style. Prescriptive ones, such as PCI DSS and CMMC, list requirements every in-scope entity must meet. Risk-based ones, such as the NIST RMF and ISO/IEC 27001, have the organization assess risk, choose controls and justify them. ISO/IEC 27001 is certifiable and uses a Statement of Applicability; its 2022 edition lists 93 controls in four themes, and ISO/IEC 27002 is the guidance on those controls. ISO/IEC 27701 adds privacy management. PCI DSS 4.0.1 has twelve requirements and is scoped to the cardholder data environment. CMMC has three levels: Level 1 protects federal contract information with 15 requirements, Level 2 covers the 110 requirements of SP 800-171 Rev. 2 for controlled unclassified information, and Level 3 adds selected SP 800-172 requirements.

Privacy laws have their own mechanics. HIPAA has Privacy, Security and Breach Notification rules and requires business associate agreements. The GDPR applies by where people are and what the company does with their data, requires notice to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a reportable breach, and can fine up to 20 million euros or 4 percent of worldwide turnover. Cloud services for federal agencies use FedRAMP, which is moving from the traditional Rev5 authorization path to FedRAMP 20x with automated, evidence-based validation. A mapping of obligations to one control set lets one control satisfy many requirements, and the program checks which obligations apply before deciding how to meet them.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to compliance sources? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of driving. Traffic law is mandatory and a police officer enforces it. Your car lease says you must service the car on schedule, which only the lender can enforce. A safe-driving course is something you choose, though your insurer might give a discount if you take it. The rules overlap, and one habit, like wearing a seat belt, can satisfy all three. A compliance program does the same sorting for security obligations.
commonTraps: PCI DSS is a contractual industry standard, not a law; FISMA, HIPAA and the GDPR are laws.
The GDPR can apply to a company outside the EU that offers services to people in the EU, and the 72 hours run from becoming aware of the breach.
CMMC Level 1 allows no POA&M, and a Level 2 conditional status needs at least 80 percent of requirements met and closure within 180 days.
An executive order directs agencies; a vendor is bound through its contract, not by the order itself.
Only ISO/IEC 27001 is certifiable; ISO/IEC 27002 is guidance on controls.
lessons.scenario: A small company hosts a web application that sells to U.S. and EU customers, takes card payments through its own servers, and has just won a subcontract to a defense prime that involves controlled unclassified information. The compliance lead lists the obligations. The GDPR applies because the company offers services to people in the EU. PCI DSS applies through the payment contracts. The subcontract flows down CMMC Level 2. The lead maps all of them to one control set, notes that one control such as multi-factor authentication satisfies several requirements, and uses ISO/IEC 27001 as the management structure.
lessons.onTheJob: The most useful artifact is an obligations register: for each requirement, the source, who enforces it, the scope, the owner, the evidence and the next due date. Contracts and customer questionnaires hide requirements that never appear in a law. When two requirements conflict, document the conflict, apply the stricter one and take legal advice, and revisit the register whenever a new product, market or data type is added.

lessons.title: Scoping the System: Boundary and Categorization
lessons.summary: Defining the authorization boundary, describing the system, categorizing its information with FIPS 199 and addressing privacy requirements.
lessons.reading:
Every later RMF step rests on one question: what exactly is the system? The authorization boundary answers it. It is the set of components managed together under one system owner and covered by one authorization. Everything inside is assessed and authorized as part of the system. Everything outside is external, and the system relies on it only through documented interconnections or inheritance. A boundary that is too small hides risk in components that were left out, and one that is too large makes authorization slow and expensive because unrelated pieces drag each other in.

Once the boundary is drawn, the team documents the system's characteristics: its purpose and functions, owners and users, environments, components, data flows, and interconnections. It also records the information types it handles. An information type is a category such as personnel records, financial data or health records. SP 800-60 helps by listing common information types with provisional impact levels. Missing a single information type is a quiet way to understate the categorization, so teams trace data flows end to end, including backups and test copies of production data.

Categorization uses FIPS 199. For each information type, and then for the system, the organization rates the impact of losing confidentiality, integrity and availability separately as low, moderate or high. Low means a limited adverse effect, moderate means a serious one, and high means a severe or catastrophic one. The system's overall category follows the high-water mark: the highest value among the three objectives and across the information types. A system rated moderate for confidentiality and availability but high for integrity is a high system. That result selects the baseline in the next step through FIPS 200.

Provisional levels from guidance can be adjusted, but only with documented justification that reflects the organization's real context, such as a much larger volume of records or a special mission need. Lowering a level only to cut the number of controls is a classic exam trap. The categorization is reviewed and approved by the authorizing official or a designee so that the result is a decision rather than a guess.

Privacy runs through scoping too. If the system touches personally identifiable information, a privacy impact assessment examines how the PII is collected, used, shared and retained, and what harm individuals could suffer. The PII confidentiality impact level considers factors such as how identifiable the data is, how much exists and how sensitive it is. Connections to other systems are recorded through interconnection agreements and, where needed, memoranda of understanding, because you cannot assume that a partner's controls match your own. Finally, the system is registered in the organization's inventory so it can be tracked and monitored.

The outline also expects the scope to be written down and the compliance required to be worked out from it. Give the system a unique name and identifier, an owner, its environments and a scope statement that says what is inside and outside the boundary. Record its purpose and functions, the missions it supports, and the stakeholders, because purpose drives how severe a loss would be. Then identify the information types and set security objectives for each one from the requirements that apply: FIPS 199 for U.S. federal systems, the organization's own risk criteria for ISO/IEC 27001, and privacy and contractual terms for personal data. Where personal data is involved, run a privacy impact assessment (U.S. federal practice) or, under the GDPR, a data protection impact assessment before processing begins; if high risk remains after mitigation, the supervisory authority must be consulted first. Other frameworks scope differently: ISO/IEC 27001 scopes the management system from context and dependencies, and PCI DSS scopes the cardholder data environment and everything connected to it. Data classification labels guide handling and should be mapped to the FIPS 199 categorization, which selects the baseline. Senior leaders review and approve the categorization before control selection begins.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to system boundaries? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Imagine fencing a property before insuring it. If you leave the garage outside the fence on the plan, a fire in the garage is a loss your policy never considered. If you draw the fence around the whole neighborhood, the policy becomes impossible to price. Categorization is the question of what is stored inside: a shed of garden tools needs a different lock than a safe full of documents, and the most valuable thing stored anywhere inside sets the level of security for the whole fenced area.
commonTraps: FIPS 199 categorizes the system; FIPS 200 sets minimum requirements and drives baseline selection. They are not interchangeable.
The overall category is the highest value across confidentiality, integrity and availability, never the average.
A dependency owned by another team is usually outside the boundary and handled through interconnection or inheritance, not simply pulled inside.
Provisional impact levels can be adjusted only with documented justification, and never merely to reduce effort.
A DPIA is done before processing starts, and high residual risk means consulting the supervisory authority first.
ISO/IEC 27001 has no fixed impact levels; do not apply the FIPS 199 levels to a question that names ISO.
lessons.scenario: A university is building a student records portal. The team lists information types: grades, financial aid details and contact information. The aid data is rated moderate for confidentiality, low for integrity and moderate for availability, but the registrar says grade changes would cause severe consequences if altered, so integrity for grades is high. A developer proposes rating the system moderate because most data is moderate. The compliance lead explains that the high integrity value sets the overall level to high, and also points out that the portal connects to a cloud payment service that must be described as an interconnection.
lessons.onTheJob: Boundary arguments usually appear when people try to dodge work. Teams carve out an awkward legacy database to shorten assessment, or lump a whole data center in to inherit its controls. Ask the question that settles most disputes: who manages it and who is accountable for it? When categorizing, bring the business owners into the room, because they know what harm looks like in their own terms. Keep a record of how each decision was reached so that the AO and later assessors can follow the reasoning.

lessons.title: Selecting and Tailoring Controls
lessons.summary: How SP 800-53 Rev. 5 and SP 800-53B baselines are chosen, tailored with overlays and common controls, and documented, including privacy controls and a monitoring strategy.
lessons.reading:
With the system categorized, the Select step chooses the safeguards. NIST SP 800-53 Revision 5 is the catalog: it describes security and privacy controls grouped into twenty families, each with a two-letter code such as AC for access control, AU for audit and accountability, CM for configuration management, IA for identification and authentication, IR for incident response and CA for assessment, authorization and monitoring. Revision 5 added PT for processing personally identifiable information and SR for supply chain risk management, and it states controls as outcomes so that they apply to many kinds of organizations.

A catalog is not a list of what to do. The baselines in SP 800-53B are the starting points. There is a Low, a Moderate and a High baseline, chosen from the overall system category through FIPS 200, and there is a privacy baseline for systems that handle PII. Starting from a baseline gives consistency and saves time, but it is only a first draft. The organization then tailors it so that it fits the system and its environment. A baseline stopped at without tailoring is usually a sign of a checklist mindset.

Tailoring has several moves. Scoping considerations remove controls that do not apply, such as a wireless control on a system with no wireless capability. Parameters, the blanks in a control such as a frequency or a list of events, are given values. Compensating controls provide comparable protection when a control cannot be met as written. Controls can be supplemented when the baseline is not enough for the risk. Common controls are identified, so that a provider such as a data center implements them once for many systems. Every removal or substitution is documented with a rationale, because the authorizing official and assessor will want to know why.

Controls differ by who implements them. A common control is implemented once and inherited. A system-specific control is implemented and managed within one system. A hybrid control is split: the organization provides one part and the system provides the other, as with incident response, where the organization supplies the process and the system supplies local procedures. Overlays go one step further. An overlay is a reusable specification that tailors a baseline for a type of system, a technology or a community, so that tailoring decisions are made once and applied consistently instead of being repeated by every team.

The output of Select is a set of plans that record how each control is planned to be implemented, who is responsible, and whether it is common, hybrid or system-specific. A system-level continuous monitoring strategy is also developed here, describing what will be monitored, how often and by whom. The authorizing official or designee reviews and approves the plans before implementation starts. Program management controls sit outside the system baselines because the organization implements them for the whole program. Other frameworks play similar roles: FedRAMP baselines for cloud services and the Statement of Applicability in ISO/IEC 27001.

The outline lists several selection details that are easy to overlook. Identify the baselines that apply (security by impact level, privacy by privacy risk) and the controls that will be inherited, and document each inherited control with the provider, its status, the part covered and the customer's remaining duties. Choose enhancements, supplement the baseline where the risk assessment requires it, and use mitigating controls when a required control cannot be met in full. Identify the data handling and marking requirements, such as the markings for controlled unclassified information, because they shape storage, transmission and disposal controls. Record each tailoring decision with its reason and approver, designate each control as system-specific, hybrid or common and allocate it to the machine, physical or human elements that carry it out, and get the owners of shared controls to agree in writing. Select the continued compliance strategy at the same time: continuous monitoring, vulnerability management, change control and reporting. The authorizing official or a designated representative then reviews and approves the plans. Other frameworks select differently: ISO/IEC 27001 uses risk treatment and a Statement of Applicability with justified exclusions, PCI DSS and CMMC set fixed requirements with only limited compensating controls or open items.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to control selection? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a hospital building a new wing. The national building code is the catalog, and a pre-printed checklist for a clinic or a surgical ward is the baseline. The architects then adjust it: no need for a helipad on a ground-floor ward, but a stronger fire door because of the oxygen stored nearby. The hospital's central power plant serves every wing, so it is a common feature, while the wing's own nurse call system is specific to it. Every adjustment goes into the building file with a reason.
commonTraps: Baselines live in SP 800-53B, not in the SP 800-53 catalog itself; Revision 5 moved them.
A compensating control replaces a control that applies but cannot be met as written; scoping removes a control that does not apply at all.
Program management controls are not allocated to Low, Moderate or High baselines; they are organization-level.
Selecting a stronger baseline everywhere is not the risk-based answer; select by impact and tailor.
Writing "inherited" is not documentation; the plan needs the provider, its status and the customer's remaining duties.
Every tailoring decision needs a recorded rationale and approval; a verbal agreement leaves no trace.
lessons.scenario: A health agency has forty small clinical applications. Each team has been tailoring the Moderate baseline separately, and assessors find that the same encryption parameters, logging frequencies and scoping decisions are different across teams for no good reason. A security architect proposes a clinical data overlay that fixes common parameter values, names the shared identity provider as a common control and requires a privacy plan for patient data. One team objects that the overlay includes a control that does not apply to their offline tool. The architect explains that the overlay allows documented scoping for exactly such a case.
lessons.onTheJob: Tailoring is where experienced practitioners earn their keep. Keep a log that ties each tailoring decision to a reason a stranger could understand, because the assessor will ask in a year when you have forgotten. Define parameter values organization-wide where you can, so that individual teams stop reinventing them. Be suspicious of compensating controls proposed in a hurry: ask what protection the original control gave and whether the substitute really delivers it. Finally, remember that a common control provider's weakness is inherited by everyone, so the quality of common controls deserves the most attention.

lessons.title: Implementing and Documenting Controls
lessons.summary: Turning planned controls into working safeguards, documenting them in the system security plan and privacy plan, and keeping evidence that they operate.
lessons.reading:
Implement is the step where plans become reality. Teams build, configure and deploy the safeguards that were chosen in Select and then document exactly what they did. The documentation is not paperwork for its own sake: the assessor will test the system against it, and the authorizing official will rely on it. For that reason a control implementation statement should say who does what, where, with which tool and how often, in terms specific enough to be checked. A statement that only repeats the control wording tells the assessor nothing.

Several principles guide implementation. Defense in depth layers different kinds of safeguards across people, process and technology, so that the failure of one does not expose the asset. Three firewalls from the same vendor are redundancy, not depth. Least privilege gives users and processes only the access they need for their tasks. Separation of duties splits sensitive actions between people, for example one person requests a change and another approves it. Secure configuration baselines, built by hardening operating systems and applications, remove default accounts and unnecessary services and make later drift visible. SP 800-128 gives guidance on security-focused configuration management.

Controls fall into administrative, technical and physical types, and into functions such as preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, recovery and compensating. A lock is preventive and physical; a log review is detective and administrative. Exam questions often describe a situation and ask for the function, so practice the difference between stopping an event, noticing it, and repairing the damage. Families worth knowing in practice include AC for access control, IA for identification and authentication including multifactor authentication, AU for audit logging, CP for contingency planning, IR for incident response, AT for training and SA for system and services acquisition.

Inheritance changes who does the work, not who is accountable. When a cloud provider or a data center supplies a control, the system owner documents that it is inherited, obtains the provider's documentation, and implements and evidences whatever remains on the customer side. Cloud providers often publish a customer responsibility matrix showing the split. Privacy controls are implemented too, including the PT family for authority, purpose, notice and consent. Federal systems generally use cryptographic modules validated under FIPS 140, not just strong algorithms. Systems security engineering, described in SP 800-160, builds trustworthiness into the design itself.

Finally, implemented does not mean effective. A control is effective when it is implemented correctly, operating as intended and producing the desired outcome. A monitoring tool that nobody watches exists, but it is not working. That is why evidence matters: configurations, logs, tickets and screenshots collected as part of normal operations show a control in action. The security and privacy plans are updated as the real system diverges from the planned one, and the control owner for each safeguard keeps its evidence current.

The outline begins this domain with a strategy, so plan before building. Choose the order of work by risk and dependencies, estimate people, tools and funding including running costs, set milestones aligned with the assessment and authorization dates, and define how effectiveness will be judged. Know the classic control types: management controls (policy, planning, risk assessment), operational controls (carried out mainly by people, such as training, physical protection and contingency procedures) and technical controls (carried out by system mechanisms), with common controls being those provided once for many systems. Set and record the frequency for reviewing policies, procedures and plans, and for literacy and role-based training; role-based training comes before access is granted, and training records are retained. Each SP 800-53 family opens with a policy and procedures control that names an official and a review cycle.

When a control cannot be implemented as written, use an approved compensating or alternate control with a documented rationale and a review date. When it cannot be fully implemented by the authorization date, record the status in the plans, the weakness and milestones in the POA&M and the residual risk in the risk register, so the authorizing official decides knowingly. Update the plans whenever the delivered implementation differs from the plan. Documentation should be proportionate and describe real practice: policies, procedures and plans that fit the organization's purpose, scope and risk profile.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to implementing controls? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture a restaurant opening a new kitchen. The health code says what must be true. Implementation is installing the sinks, setting the fridge temperatures, training the cooks and writing down who checks the fridges and when. Layers matter: cold storage, handwashing and cooking temperatures each catch what the others miss. Giving every cook a key to the manager's office would break least privilege, and letting the same person order, receive and pay for stock would break separation of duties. The inspector will later ask for the temperature logs, not just the policy.
commonTraps: Redundant copies of the same control are not defense in depth; depth means different layers.
Least privilege limits what each person can do; separation of duties splits a task among people. They are separate principles.
A strong algorithm does not equal FIPS validated cryptography; the module must be validated.
Inheriting a control from a provider does not remove the system owner's duty to document and verify it.
A control that exists but is not monitored or tested may be implemented but not effective.
A risk register tracks risks and decisions; the POA&M tracks remediation work and dates.
Management, operational and technical describe the nature of a control; common describes who implements it.
lessons.scenario: A logistics company runs its order system in a public cloud. In review, the assessor finds that the plan states audit logging is handled by the provider, while the provider's responsibility matrix says the customer must collect and review application logs. Nobody has been reviewing them, and a single administrator can both deploy code and approve its release. The team had considered logging a solved problem because a tool was purchased. After the finding, the system owner assigns control owners, rewrites the implementation statements and adds approvals by a second person for releases.
lessons.onTheJob: Write implementation statements as though you are explaining the system to a new colleague who must test it. Name tools, roles, frequencies and where evidence lives. Assign a named control owner to every control, because unowned controls decay quietly. When a provider supplies part of a control, get its current documentation and map it to your boundary on day one, not the week before assessment. And collect evidence as a by-product of normal operations, so that proof of a control is a log you already have, not a document you assemble in a panic.

lessons.title: Assessing and Auditing Controls
lessons.summary: Planning and conducting control assessments with SP 800-53A, reporting findings in the SAR and tracking weaknesses in a POA&M.
lessons.reading:
Assessment answers a plain question: do the controls work? NIST SP 800-53A Revision 5 supplies assessment procedures that match each control in SP 800-53, so assessors do not invent their own tests. The assessor, whether an internal team or a third party, is chosen for a level of independence that the authorizing official decides. Higher-impact systems call for more independence, because results done by the people who built the system are less credible. An assessor is a fact-finder, not a decision maker about risk.

Everything begins with the security assessment plan. It names the controls and objectives to be assessed, the methods and objects to be used, the assessors, the schedule and the rules of engagement. The plan is approved by the system owner or authorizing official before testing starts. Rules of engagement matter most for hands-on testing: they say what may be touched, when, with which techniques and whom to call if something breaks. Testing outside the plan, for example running an exploit against a server that was never listed, risks disrupting production and exceeding authority.

SP 800-53A defines three assessment methods. Examine reviews specifications, such as policies and plans, and also configurations and records. Interview discusses the control with the people who carry it out. Test exercises a mechanism and compares actual behavior with expected behavior. The things assessed are called assessment objects: specifications, mechanisms, activities and individuals. Methods pair with objects, so you test a firewall mechanism and interview the administrator. Documents and interviews show intent and belief; for technical controls, only examination of the real configuration or testing shows what is true. Assessors may also use sampling, in which case the plan explains how the sample was chosen.

Findings are recorded objectively, with each objective judged satisfied or other than satisfied and the reasoning noted. Vulnerability scans support the work, but results need validation because scanners produce false positives. Penetration tests go further by showing whether weaknesses can really be exploited. If the team fixes something during the assessment, the report still documents the original finding and the retest, because the report is a record of what was found, not of what the team wishes had been found. Effective controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended and producing the desired outcome, and an assessor looks at all three.

The results go into the security assessment report. Weaknesses that remain are placed in a plan of action and milestones, which lists each one with the resources required, the person responsible, milestones and completion dates. A POA&M is a commitment to fix, not permission to ignore. Privacy controls are assessed alongside security controls, including whether PII is processed only as documented. Outside the federal world, assessment appears as audits and attestations: a FedRAMP 3PAO assessment, a SOC 2 Type II report that tests operation over a period, or an ISO/IEC 27001 certification audit. All answer the same question for different audiences.

The outline treats assessment and audit as six tasks, so know what belongs in each. Preparation sets stakeholder roles, objectives, scope, resources, schedule, deliverables and logistics, scopes assets, methods and level of effort (depth and coverage grow with risk and impact), reviews earlier assessments and documentation, and ends with an approved plan. Conducting the assessment applies examine, interview and test, where testing can be control testing, vulnerability scanning or penetration testing (SP 800-115 groups techniques into review, target identification and analysis, and target vulnerability validation), and the evidence is verified and validated by corroboration. The initial report records risks, risk mitigation summaries and preliminary findings. Reviewing it means assigning a response to each finding (avoid, accept, share, mitigate or transfer) in collaboration with stakeholders, and reassessing corrective actions before closing a finding. The final report states compliant, non-compliant or not applicable with reasons, records recommendations and is finalized after review for accuracy. The risk response plan lists residual risks and deficiencies, ranks them by risk, and estimates the resources and time to mitigate each, which becomes the POA&M.

Audits add vocabulary: first-party (internal), second-party (customer or partner) and third-party (independent) audits, and findings classified as major or minor nonconformities or observations, with corrective action and verification. A control that was not tested is a coverage gap, not a not applicable result, and an other than satisfied finding can also mean the evidence was insufficient.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to control assessment? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a vehicle inspection. The inspector follows a published checklist, not personal taste, and must not be the mechanic who just repaired the car. Before starting, the inspector and the owner agree what will be checked. Reading the maintenance log is examining, asking the owner when the brakes were last serviced is interviewing, and driving the car through a brake test is testing. The final report lists what passed and what failed, and the owner gets a repair list with dates, which is the equivalent of the POA&M.
commonTraps: The assessor reports findings and does not accept risk or decide authorization.
The plan is approved before testing; the SAR and POA&M come from the results.
Interviews and policy reviews show intent; technical controls need examination of configurations or testing.
A scan is not a penetration test, and unvalidated scan output is not an assessment.
A SOC 2 Type I report covers design at a point in time; only Type II tests operation over a period.
A control that was not tested is a coverage gap; it is neither compliant nor not applicable.
Findings are recorded from evidence; management may disagree, but the disagreement is recorded rather than the finding deleted.
lessons.scenario: A defense contractor is assessed by an internal team that reports to the system owner. The assessor finds that remote access logging was not enabled for several weeks. The system owner asks for the finding to be removed because it was fixed before the report was issued. The lead assessor refuses to delete it but agrees to record the finding, the fix and the successful retest. The authorizing official later asks whether the team was independent enough, and the organization decides that for this high-impact system an assessor from outside the program will be used next time.
lessons.onTheJob: Treat the assessment plan as the contract that protects everyone. Get written approval for the scope and methods, and confirm emergency contacts before any hands-on testing. Do not let schedule pressure change a finding: the report is more valuable when it is honest, and authorizing officials who see candid reports trust the process. When the scan output arrives, spend the time to validate the top findings before sending it on. And write the POA&M as a working document with owners and dates, because the AO will read it as a statement of how seriously you take the weaknesses.

lessons.title: Authorization and the Authorizing Official Decision
lessons.summary: Assembling the authorization package, analyzing risk and issuing ATO, ATU or DATO decisions, with FedRAMP and common control authorization.
lessons.reading:
The Authorize step is where a named official accepts the risk of operating the system. It starts with the authorization package, which gives the authorizing official what is needed to decide: the security and privacy plans, the assessment reports, the plan of action and milestones, and an executive summary. In everyday language people call this the SSP, SAR and POA&M package. The package is assembled before the decision, and if its documents are incomplete or out of date, the AO is deciding on stale facts.

Risk analysis and determination comes next. The organization looks at the weaknesses found, the controls in place, the plans to fix the rest and the threats the system faces, and decides what residual risk would remain if the system operated. That residual risk is then compared with the organization's risk tolerance. This is a judgment about operations, assets, individuals and other organizations, not a count of findings. Risk response options, such as mitigation or acceptance, are considered, and preferred courses of action are identified. Skipping straight from the assessment to approval because the project is late is the wrong answer on the exam and in practice.

The authorizing official then issues a decision. An authorization to operate says the risk is acceptable, usually for a defined period or under ongoing authorization, and can carry conditions such as closing particular POA&M items by specific dates. A denial of authorization to operate says the risk is not acceptable, so the system must not operate or must stop. A denial is a legitimate outcome, and the AO who issues one is doing the job. An authorization to use lets an agency rely on another organization's authorization for a system or service, such as a cloud service, while making its own risk decision. A common control authorization approves shared controls so that many systems can inherit them.

Authorizations do not last forever. An authorization termination date sets the end of the risk acceptance unless it is renewed. Reauthorization is a new decision after significant change or expiry. Ongoing authorization allows the AO to continue accepting risk based on information from a mature monitoring program, with no periodic reauthorization, but it works only if that program really produces current data. Conditions of authorization are enforceable: if they are not met, the AO may modify or revoke the decision.

In the cloud world, FedRAMP standardizes assessment and authorization of cloud services for federal use. Its baselines come from NIST SP 800-53, an independent third-party assessment organization performs the assessment, and the principle is do once, use many times. An agency still makes its own decision to use the service. Privacy compliance runs in parallel: the Privacy Act requires agencies to publish a system of records notice when records are retrieved by personal identifier. And remember that compliance is not the same as security. A checklist can be met while real risk remains, so the best answers address both the requirement and the underlying risk.

The outline breaks this domain into documents, risk posture and notification. For documents, compile and review the package for completeness and consistency, then submit it to the party who decides: the authorizing official or designated representative for a federal system, a sponsoring agency or the FedRAMP program office for a cloud service, a certification body for ISO/IEC 27001, an acquirer or card brand for PCI DSS. For risk posture, apply the organization's risk acceptance criteria, determine residual risk for each weakness and in aggregate (weaknesses that share an attack path can combine into a higher risk), obtain concurrence from stakeholders who are affected, including owners of connected and inheriting systems, and record the residual risk formally with rationale, conditions, owner and date. Concurrence does not move accountability; the authorizing official still decides. For notification, issue a signed written decision with the decision type, conditions and dates, share it with the system owner, control owners, common control providers, inheriting systems and risk oversight officials, and keep external statements accurate about scope and status. Other frameworks use different instruments: a certificate from a certification body, an attestation of compliance, an auditor's report or a status recorded in a government system.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to authorization decisions? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of an airline's sign-off before a new aircraft enters service. The inspectors hand over a file: the maintenance plan, the inspection report and a list of open repair items with dates. The chief accountable official reads it, weighs the risks against what the airline is willing to accept, and signs for a limited period with conditions, or refuses to sign. If another airline already certified the same aircraft type, a second airline can review that file and decide to use it, but the second airline's chief still signs for their own fleet.
commonTraps: The authorization decision accepts risk; it does not certify that the system is perfectly secure.
A denial is a valid outcome and does not mean the process failed.
An authorization to use is a decision by the using agency; it is not an automatic inheritance from the first agency.
Ongoing authorization depends on a mature continuous monitoring program; without it, there is no basis.
Stakeholder concurrence shows agreement; the authorizing official still decides and stays accountable.
A risk accepted verbally is undocumented; acceptance must be written, signed and dated.
lessons.scenario: A regional utility's billing system has finished assessment with one high weakness that can be fixed in six weeks and several moderate weaknesses with a credible plan. The project manager wants an authorization to operate today because the billing cycle begins next week. The AO reads the package, notes compensating monitoring for the high weakness and the funded plan, and issues an authorization to operate with the condition that the high item close within 60 days, and with a termination date one year out. The AO states that failing the condition will trigger a reassessment of the decision.
lessons.onTheJob: Authorizing officials are busy, so build the package for them: a one-page executive summary with the real residual risk in plain words, a POA&M that is honest about dates, and a clear recommendation of the decision options. Do not bury a serious weakness in an appendix, because AOs who feel surprised later become cautious about everything you send. When you receive a DATO, treat it as information, fix the cause and resubmit. And track conditions in the POA&M with owners so that an expired condition never goes unnoticed.

lessons.title: Keeping the Authorization Alive
lessons.summary: Continuous monitoring, change control, security impact analysis, ongoing risk response, reporting and system disposal under SP 800-137.
lessons.reading:
An authorization is a snapshot, and systems change every day. The Monitor step keeps the authorization meaningful by maintaining awareness of the system's security and privacy posture and of its environment. Information security continuous monitoring, described in NIST SP 800-137, replaces the old habit of assessing everything every few years with ongoing, risk-based assessment of controls. Its purpose is to give decision makers current information so that they can accept, reduce or avoid risk with their eyes open.

SP 800-137 describes a cycle. First define a monitoring strategy tied to the organization's risk tolerance. Then establish the program, deciding metrics, frequencies and responsibilities. Then implement it, collecting data through automated tools and manual checks. Analyze and report the findings in a form leaders can use, respond to the findings, and review and update the program as threats, technology and mission change. The frequency for each control depends on its volatility, the system's impact level, available threat and vulnerability information, how critical the control is, known weaknesses and the organization's risk tolerance. Not every control needs the same schedule.

Change is the largest source of new risk. A change control process, often run by a configuration control board, requests, reviews, approves, implements and records changes against the baseline configuration. Before the change, a security and privacy impact analysis asks how it affects the system's posture and whether more assessment is needed. A significant change, such as a new interconnection, a major architecture change or a move to a different cloud provider, may require reassessment or even reauthorization. Organizations define thresholds for significance in policy, because the judgment is about risk, not the number of servers touched. Unmanaged change produces configuration drift, which quietly undoes hardening and invalidates earlier assessment results.

Monitoring finds problems, and response fixes them. Ongoing risk response mitigates, accepts, shares or avoids what is discovered, and the plans and POA&M are updated so that the authorization package stays accurate. Vulnerability and patch management work in the background, prioritized by risk rather than by trying to fix everything at once. Third parties deserve the same attention: contract rights to audit and to receive incident notice, together with periodic review of assurance reports, give real oversight of external providers. Contingency plans are exercised and updated, and lessons learned from incidents feed back into the strategy.

Reporting closes the loop. The authorizing official and other leaders receive regular reports on the security and privacy posture, in summary form that supports decisions. Metrics such as patch latency or the number of overdue POA&M items help, provided someone acts on them. When the monitoring program is mature, the AO may move from periodic reauthorization to ongoing authorization. Finally, systems end. Disposal retires the system in an orderly way: notify stakeholders, handle data and media according to sensitivity using methods from SP 800-88, remove interconnections, update inventory and keep the records required.
