The outline splits this domain into change management, ongoing compliance, audit support and decommissioning. Change management weighs each change against risk, operations and compliance (including revisions to baselines), documents it and has authorized personnel such as a change control board approve it, deploys through environments such as development, test and production with a rollback plan, and tracks every change so that unapproved ones are detected and enforced against; emergency changes use a faster path and are reviewed afterward. Ongoing compliance sets how often activities are reviewed with stakeholders, monitors physical and logical assets, personnel and change control, keeps incident response and contingency capabilities exercised and current, applies security updates and tracks remediation to closure, collects evidence and updates documents including service level agreements and third-party contracts, repeats awareness and role-based training and keeps the records, and revises the monitoring strategy when laws, regulations, suppliers or requirements change.

Audit support means performing the required testing and vulnerability scanning on the cadence the framework sets (PCI DSS, for example, expects quarterly external scans by an approved scanning vendor and penetration testing at least annually), interviewing the people who operate controls, and reviewing and updating documentation afterward. Decommissioning reviews the requirements with stakeholders (data retention, legal holds, dependencies), removes the system from operation by disconnecting interconnections, revoking access, sanitizing media under SP 800-88 Rev. 2 and updating inventories, and retains and shares the records, such as the decommissioning plan, sanitization certificates and the termination notice.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to continuous monitoring? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A building that passed its fire inspection in January is not safe forever. Someone props open a fire door, a storage room fills with boxes, a new tenant adds extension cords. The facility manager keeps a schedule: check the sprinklers monthly, the extinguishers every quarter, and review any renovation plan before work starts. Reports go to the owner, who decides what to fix first. When the building is torn down, the owner makes sure nothing hazardous is left behind. The ongoing routine, not the January inspection alone, is what keeps people safe.
commonTraps: A security impact analysis is performed before a change, not after it.
Continuous monitoring is risk-based and does not mean assessing every control constantly.
Formatting a drive is not media sanitization for sensitive data; SP 800-88 methods apply.
Ongoing authorization is only valid when a continuous monitoring program provides current information.
A change without an approved record is unauthorized even if it was sensible; emergencies move the paperwork, not the accountability.
A legal hold overrides scheduled disposal and sanitization when a system is decommissioned.
lessons.scenario: A bank's loan processing system is moving from its own data center to a managed cloud platform. The system owner treats it as routine because the application does not change. The ISSM points out that the hosting move changes inherited controls, interconnections and logging, and that the organization's policy calls such a move a significant change. A security impact analysis finds several controls will need reassessment. The AO decides on a targeted reassessment rather than a full one, updates the conditions of the authorization and asks for monthly posture reports during the transition.
lessons.onTheJob: Make monitoring boring and automated. The programs that fail are the ones that depend on a single person remembering to run something. Tie every metric to a decision, and kill the ones nobody uses. Get change management involved from day one, since most surprises arrive as changes nobody told security about. Keep the SSP and POA&M current as part of closing each change ticket, not as a quarterly cleanup. And when a system retires, own the decommissioning checklist: data, media, accounts, connections, inventory and records.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam format and domain weights
points: The outline (effective June 15, 2024) has seven domains: 1 Program 16%, 2 Scope of the System 10%, 3 Selection and Approval of Controls 14%, 4 Implementation 17%, 5 Assessment/Audit 16%, 6 System Compliance 14%, 7 Compliance Maintenance 13%.
125 items in 3 hours at a Pearson VUE testing center; multiple choice and advanced item types; passing score 700 out of 1000; English.
Experience: two years cumulative paid work in one or more of the seven domains. A candidate who passes without the experience becomes an Associate of ISC2 and has three years to earn it.
Implementation (17%) and Program (16%) plus Assessment/Audit (16%) together carry almost half the exam; Scope is the smallest domain.

cheatSheet.heading: RMF at a glance
points: Seven steps: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor (SP 800-37 Rev. 2).
Prepare works at organization and system level; the other steps are system-focused.
Outputs by step: system description and categorization, tailored plans, implemented controls, SAP and SAR, POA&M, authorization package and decision, monitoring reports.
The RMF is a process; SP 800-53 is the catalog, SP 800-53B the baselines, SP 800-53A the assessment procedures.

cheatSheet.heading: Roles and who decides what
points: Authorizing official: accepts risk and issues the authorization decision.
Risk executive function: organization-wide, consistent risk oversight across systems.
System owner: owns the system and its plans. ISSO/ISSM: day-to-day security. Control owner: operates a control.
Security control assessor: evaluates and reports; does not accept risk. Independence level is set by the AO.
SAOP: privacy program accountability. Common control provider: supplies inherited controls.

cheatSheet.heading: Risk management essentials
points: SP 800-39: three tiers (organization, mission and business process, system) and four components (frame, assess, respond, monitor).
SP 800-30: prepare, conduct, communicate, maintain; risk combines threat, vulnerability, likelihood and impact.
Responses: accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer. Transfer does not remove accountability.
Risk tolerance is set by leadership in the risk management strategy.

cheatSheet.heading: Categorization
points: FIPS 199: low (limited), moderate (serious), high (severe or catastrophic) for confidentiality, integrity and availability.
High-water mark: the highest value sets the overall level; never average.
SP 800-60: information types and provisional impact levels; adjust only with justification.
PII: privacy impact assessment, SP 800-122 PII confidentiality impact level.

cheatSheet.heading: Control selection
points: SP 800-53 Rev. 5: 20 families, privacy integrated, PT and SR families added; baselines in SP 800-53B.
FIPS 200: 17 minimum security requirement areas; baseline chosen by impact level.
Tailoring: scoping, parameters, compensating, supplementation, common control designation, overlays.
Common, hybrid and system-specific describe who implements; PM controls are organization-level.

cheatSheet.heading: Implementation and documentation
points: SSP and privacy plan describe boundary, categorization, and how each control is implemented.
Defense in depth means diverse layers; least privilege limits access; separation of duties splits tasks.
Inheritance does not remove responsibility; customer responsibility matrix defines the split.
Effective means implemented correctly, operating as intended and producing the desired outcome.

cheatSheet.heading: Assessment and audit
points: SAP before testing (with rules of engagement); SAR after; POA&M for remaining weaknesses.
Methods: examine, interview, test; objects: specifications, mechanisms, activities, individuals.
Scans need validation; penetration tests show exploitability. SOC 2 Type II tests operation over time.
FedRAMP uses a 3PAO. ISO/IEC 27001 certification uses an accredited body and a Statement of Applicability.

cheatSheet.heading: Authorization and monitoring
points: Package: security and privacy plans, assessment reports, POA&M, executive summary.
Decisions: ATO (acceptable risk), DATO (not acceptable), ATU (rely on another organization's package), common control authorization.
ISCM (SP 800-137): define, establish, implement, analyze and report, respond, review and update; frequency is risk-based.
Impact analysis before changes; significant change may need reassessment; disposal uses SP 800-88 sanitization.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: Format: 125 items in 3 hours, multiple choice and advanced item types; a score of 700 out of 1000 points is needed to pass. Confirm the current details on the ISC2 site before booking.
Time: about 85 seconds per question. Skip nothing for long; mark and return.
Phrasing: BEST, FIRST and MOST appropriate questions have several plausible answers. Pick the one that follows the process order and the defined roles.
Default to the authorizing official for risk acceptance, the assessor for facts, the system owner for the plans, and the RMF step order for what comes first.
Eliminate answers that skip a step, bypass approval or put risk acceptance in the wrong role.

madlibs.scenario: Leadership sets how much risk the organization will accept in pursuit of its mission, which is called risk {b1}. When a hosting contract moves part of the financial loss to an insurer, that risk response is {b2}, but the organization still remains accountable for protecting the data.

options: tolerance
baseline
boundary
impact
mitigation
transfer or sharing
avoidance
acceptance

madlibs.explanation: Risk tolerance is a leadership decision recorded in the risk management strategy. Transferring or sharing moves part of the financial impact, not the responsibility for protecting the information.

madlibs.scenario: A team rates a system {b1} for confidentiality, low for integrity and low for availability. Following the {b2} rule, the overall system level used to choose the control baseline is therefore moderate. The standard that defines these three impact levels is FIPS {b3}.

options: moderate
high
limited
serious
high-water mark
least privilege
separation of duties
defense in depth

madlibs.explanation: Each objective is rated separately and the highest value sets the overall level, so moderate confidentiality with low integrity and availability gives a moderate system. FIPS 199 defines the levels; FIPS 200 handles minimum requirements.

madlibs.scenario: The starting set of controls for a given impact level is called a {b1}, and the document that publishes the Low, Moderate and High sets is NIST SP 800-{b2}. When a control does not apply because the system has no such capability, the team applies a {b3} consideration.

options: baseline
overlay

family
scoping
compensating
supplemental
inheritance

madlibs.explanation: Baselines are published in SP 800-53B. SP 800-53A holds assessment procedures. Scoping removes controls that do not apply, whereas a compensating control substitutes for one that applies but cannot be met as written.

madlibs.scenario: A cloud provider supplies physical security that many tenants rely on, so the tenant treats it as an {b1} control and documents it. The part of the control the tenant must configure itself remains the tenant's duty, which is why the provider publishes a customer {b2} matrix.

options: inherited
compensating
optional
deterrent
responsibility
impact

risk

madlibs.explanation: Inherited controls come from a provider, but the customer still documents and evidences its own portion, which the customer responsibility matrix identifies.

madlibs.scenario: Before testing, the assessor and system owner agree on a security assessment {b1} that sets out scope, methods and the rules of engagement. After testing, the findings are written into the security assessment {b2}, and weaknesses that remain are tracked in a {b3}.

options: plan
report
package
strategy
report
plan

boundary

statement of applicability
system of records notice

madlibs.explanation: The plan comes before testing, the report records results, and the POA&M tracks remediation of remaining weaknesses.

madlibs.scenario: The official with authority to accept risk for a system is the {b1} official. If the residual risk is within tolerance, that official issues an authorization to {b2}, and if it is not, the decision is a {b3}.

options: authorizing
assessing
privacy
executive
operate
assess

monitor
denial of authorization to operate
system disposal

madlibs.explanation: The authorizing official owns risk acceptance. An ATO accepts risk for operation, and a DATO is the legitimate outcome when residual risk is unacceptable.

madlibs.scenario: A controller learns of a personal data breach that is likely to put individuals at risk. It must notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within {b1} of becoming aware. The same law allows fines of up to {b2} of worldwide annual turnover for the most serious infringements.

30 days
60 days
7 days
4 percent

madlibs.scenario: Before starting large-scale profiling that is likely to be high risk to individuals, the GDPR requires a {b1}. If high residual risk remains after mitigation, the controller must {b2} before processing begins.

options: data protection impact assessment
penetration test
SOC 2 report
business impact analysis
consult the supervisory authority
wait for the first complaint
notify the card brands
obtain an authorization to operate

madlibs.scenario: A change request should include an impact analysis, test results, approval by authorized personnel such as a {b1}, and a {b2} so the change can be reversed if deployment fails.

options: change control board
help desk
marketing team
vendor sales team
rollback plan
press release
password reset
new boundary

madlibs.explanation: Authorized approvers such as a change control board decide on changes, and a rollback plan is prepared before deployment so that a failed change can be backed out.

sequences.prompt: Put the seven RMF steps in the correct order.
steps: Prepare
Categorize
Select
Implement
Assess
Authorize
Monitor
sequences.explanation: Prepare sets context first, categorization defines what must be protected, selection chooses controls to match, implementation builds them, assessment tests them, authorization accepts the residual risk, and monitoring keeps the authorization meaningful.

sequences.prompt: Put these scoping activities in the usual order for a new system.
steps: Define the authorization boundary and describe the system
Identify the information types the system handles
Rate confidentiality, integrity and availability impact for each type
Apply the high-water mark to set the overall system category
Review and approve the categorization and register the system
sequences.explanation: You must know what the system is before you can list its information, rate impact, determine the overall level and have the result approved and recorded.

sequences.prompt: Put these steps for selecting controls in the correct order.
steps: Select the baseline that matches the system impact level
Tailor the baseline using scoping, parameters and compensating controls
Allocate controls as common, hybrid or system-specific
Document the planned implementation in the security and privacy plans
Develop the system-level continuous monitoring strategy
Review and approve the plans
sequences.explanation: The baseline comes first, then tailoring, then allocation to who implements what. The plan records it all and the monitoring strategy follows from it. Approval comes last so the AO approves the finished set.

sequences.prompt: Put the assessment and remediation activities in the correct order.
steps: Select the assessor or assessment team
Develop and approve the security assessment plan
Conduct the assessment and gather evidence
Prepare the security assessment report
Perform initial remediation and retest
Prepare the plan of action and milestones for remaining weaknesses
sequences.explanation: The assessor is chosen first, and the plan is approved before testing. Results go into the report, quick fixes are retested, and only the weaknesses that remain are tracked in the POA&M.

sequences.prompt: Put the authorization workflow in the correct order.
steps: Assemble the authorization package
Analyze the package and determine risk
Identify the preferred risk response
The authorizing official makes the authorization decision
Report the decision to the stakeholders
sequences.explanation: The package supplies the facts, the risk determination interprets them, the response is chosen, the AO decides, and the decision is communicated.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps of a controlled system change in the correct order.
steps: Submit the change request
Analyze impact on risk, operations and compliance
Obtain approval from the change control board
Test in a non-production environment
Deploy with the rollback plan ready
Verify the result and update baseline and records
sequences.explanation: A change is requested, analyzed, approved, tested away from production, deployed with a way back, and then verified with the baseline and records updated.

sequences.prompt: Put the six assessment or audit tasks in the correct order.
steps: Prepare for the assessment or audit
Conduct the assessment or audit
Prepare the initial report
Review the initial report and plan risk response actions
Develop the final report
Develop the risk response plan
sequences.explanation: The outline orders the tasks from preparation, through testing and an initial report, to review and response, the final report and the plan for residual risk.

sequences.prompt: Put the decommissioning activities in a sensible order.
steps: Review requirements with stakeholders
Notify users and plan the retirement
Disconnect interconnections and revoke access
Archive or sanitize data and media
Remove the system from inventory and monitoring
Retain and share the decommissioning records
sequences.explanation: Requirements and dependencies are settled first, then the system is disconnected and its data handled, then the registers are updated and records are kept.

caseStudies.title: Harborview Clinic's Patient Portal
caseStudies.scenario: Harborview Clinic is building a patient portal that lets patients view lab results, message clinicians and pay bills. The portal runs on a managed cloud platform whose provider supplies the data center and the underlying network. It connects to the clinic's electronic health record system, run by another department with its own owner, and to a card payment service. Analysts list information types: clinical results, billing records and contact details. A privacy officer notes that messages may include free-text health information. The team rates clinical results as high for confidentiality, moderate for integrity and moderate for availability, and rates billing as moderate for confidentiality, low for integrity and low for availability. A developer wants to rate the system moderate overall because the billing data is moderate. A test copy of production data is kept in a separate cloud project for the developers. The project sponsor asks the team to finish categorization and boundary work before the next planning meeting.

questions.question: What overall category should the system have for baseline selection?
options: Moderate, because billing and most objectives are moderate
High, because the highest value governs
Moderate, because the average of the ratings is moderate
Low, because integrity and availability for billing are low
questions.explanation: The high-water mark takes the highest value across objectives and information types, so high confidentiality for clinical results sets the system level to high. Averaging or following the majority understates the impact.

questions.question: How should the electronic health record system run by another department be treated?
options: Outside the boundary, with an interconnection agreement
As unrelated because another department owns it
As a common control provided by the cloud platform
As inside the boundary because the portal depends on it
questions.explanation: A component with a different owner is generally outside the boundary and handled through a documented interconnection. Including it makes the portal owner accountable for something they do not manage, ignoring it hides risk, and it is not part of the platform provider's inherited controls.

questions.question: The test copy of production data in a separate cloud project can be left out of scoping because it is used only by developers.
questions.explanation: The copy holds production data, so it carries the same sensitivity and must be considered in the boundary and categorization, or the data must be removed or masked. Use by developers does not reduce impact.

questions.question: Which two actions best address privacy during scoping? (Choose two.)
options: Treat privacy as a separate project to be handled after launch
Rely on the cloud provider's privacy policy alone
Consider the PII confidentiality impact level, including identifiability and sensitivity
Skip privacy because encryption will be used
Conduct a privacy impact assessment of how PII will be collected and used
questions.explanation: A privacy impact assessment and a PII impact consideration inform controls early. Encryption does not decide lawful processing, postponing privacy leaves requirements unmet, and a provider's policy does not cover the clinic's own obligations.

caseStudies.title: Ridgeline Air Traffic Analytics Authorization
caseStudies.scenario: Ridgeline Analytics supports a federal aviation agency with a flight data analysis system categorized as moderate. After assessment, the report shows two high weaknesses and nine moderate ones. One high weakness concerns unreviewed administrative activity logs and can be fixed in four weeks. The other relates to an unsupported component in a vendor library, and the vendor has promised a fix in three months. The POA&M shows owners, funds and dates, and compensating monitoring is in place for the vendor component. The system also relies on a common control, physical security, provided by the agency data center, which has a current common control authorization. The authorizing official is told the system is needed for the next quarter's operations. The project manager wants an authorization to operate without conditions, saying that delays have already cost two months. The assessor, who is independent of the project, recommends that the AO require the log review fix as a condition. A second agency is interested in using the same system for its own analysts. The AO asks for a risk summary and the planned continuous monitoring approach before deciding.

questions.question: What is the most appropriate decision type for the AO if residual risk is within tolerance?
options: Authorization to use, since another agency is interested
Authorization to operate with no conditions to avoid more delay
Authorization to operate with conditions tied to the POA&M items
Denial of authorization to operate because high weaknesses exist
questions.explanation: A risk-based AO may authorize operation and attach enforceable conditions. Denial for any high weakness is not required when risk is acceptable, no conditions ignores the plan and the assessor's recommendation, and ATU is a decision a using agency makes about someone else's system.

questions.question: The assessor should decide whether the AO accepts the risk, since the assessor is independent and knows the findings.
questions.explanation: Independence makes the findings credible, but risk acceptance belongs to the AO.

questions.question: The second agency wants to rely on the first agency's package. Which decision does the second agency make?
options: A denial, because the system is not its own
Authorization to use, made by its own AO after reviewing the package
No decision, since the first authorization is inherited automatically
Common control authorization, issued by the first agency
questions.explanation: Authorization to use lets an agency rely on existing documentation but make its own risk decision. Common control authorization covers shared controls, and no decision is not an option because accountability for the risk stays with the using agency.

questions.question: Which two items strengthen the basis for moving from periodic reauthorization to ongoing authorization later? (Choose two.)
options: Raising the termination date without review
Reducing the frequency of assessments for all controls
Removing the POA&M requirement
Regular posture reporting to the AO with updated plans and POA&M
A mature continuous monitoring program that provides current risk information
questions.explanation: Ongoing authorization depends on current, reliable information and regular reporting. Removing the POA&M, extending dates without review and reducing assessment frequency would remove the basis for decisions.

compare.scenario: A new agency system will process sensitive data. Before any system is categorized, a project sponsor asks how to prevent officials from reaching inconsistent risk decisions. Which is the better answer?
compare.optionA: Establish an organization-wide risk management strategy that states risk tolerance and decision rights
compare.optionB: Ask each authorizing official to document their own assumptions in each system security plan
compare.why: A shared strategy sets a common basis for decisions before systems are assessed. Having each AO document assumptions is the tempting runner-up because it feels transparent, but it records the inconsistency instead of preventing it.

compare.scenario: A manager finds that a supplier's cloud service will hold company data and wants the strongest basis for ongoing governance. Which is better?
compare.optionA: Send the supplier an annual security questionnaire and file the answers
compare.optionB: Include audit and incident notification rights in the contract and review assurance reports periodically
compare.why: Contract rights and independent assurance allow real verification. The questionnaire is the tempting runner-up because it is simple, but self-reported answers once a year give thin oversight and no ability to compel evidence.

compare.scenario: A team categorizes a system with moderate confidentiality, high integrity and moderate availability. Which overall level should be used to select the baseline?
compare.optionA: Moderate, because most of the objectives are moderate
compare.optionB: High, because the highest of the three objective values sets the level
compare.why: The high-water mark applies. Moderate is the runner-up because it matches the majority, but the standard does not use majority or averages; a single high objective raises the whole system.

compare.scenario: A new application depends on an identity service run by another business unit. How should the boundary treat it?
compare.optionA: Keep it outside the boundary and document the interconnection or inheritance
compare.optionB: Bring it inside the boundary so it gets assessed with this application
compare.why: Components managed under a different owner are generally outside and handled through documented interconnection or inheritance. Including it is tempting because it seems thorough, but the application owner cannot manage or accept risk for components they do not control.

compare.scenario: A legacy system cannot enforce a baseline password setting. Which is the better handling?
compare.optionA: Remove the control from the baseline because the system cannot support it
compare.optionB: Document a compensating control with justification and have it assessed
compare.why: A compensating control preserves comparable protection and stays under assessment. Removal is the tempting runner-up because it is quick, but it leaves the need unaddressed and no one has accepted the resulting risk.

compare.scenario: Many similar systems at an agency repeat the same tailoring debates. Which is the better solution?
compare.optionA: Develop an overlay with agreed parameters and scoping decisions
compare.optionB: Move all systems to the High baseline to avoid debates
compare.why: An overlay records tailoring once, consistently. The High baseline is the tempting runner-up because it ends arguments, but it ignores risk-based selection and adds cost for controls that bring little benefit.

compare.scenario: A provider supplies a control that the customer inherits. Which is the better practice for the customer system owner?
compare.optionA: Record the control as inherited and take no further action
compare.optionB: Obtain the provider's current documentation and document and evidence the customer-side responsibilities
compare.why: Inheritance does not remove the owner's duty to verify fit and cover their own portion. Simply recording it is the tempting runner-up, but it leaves the customer-side gaps and stale provider information unchecked.

compare.scenario: An assessor wants to confirm that account lockout is configured as described. Which approach gives better assurance?
compare.optionA: Review the policy and interview the administrator
compare.optionB: Examine the configuration and test lockout behavior
compare.why: Technical controls need evidence of actual behavior. The policy review and interview are the tempting runner-up because they are quick, but they show intent and belief, not operation.

compare.scenario: An AO receives a package with a serious but fixable weakness and a credible plan. Residual risk is within tolerance. Which decision is better?
compare.optionA: Deny authorization until every weakness is fully resolved
compare.optionB: Authorize operation with conditions tied to closing the weakness by a set date
compare.why: The AO decides on residual risk against tolerance. Denial is the tempting runner-up for caution, but a risk-based decision can allow operation under conditions when the risk is acceptable, which keeps the mission running without ignoring the weakness.

compare.scenario: A system owner plans to add a new interconnection next month. Which is better?
compare.optionA: Perform a security and privacy impact analysis before approving the change
compare.optionB: Make the change and update the plan if the next scan shows a problem
compare.why: Impact analysis before a change shows whether reassessment is needed. Waiting for a scan is the tempting runner-up because it seems efficient, but it discovers problems after exposure has already begun.

compare.scenario: An authorizing official finds that two moderate weaknesses on the same internet-facing subsystem could be chained into one attack path. Which judgment is better?
compare.optionA: Assess the combined effect of the weaknesses against the organization's risk tolerance
compare.optionB: Rate each weakness on its own and accept both because each is only moderate
compare.why: Aggregate residual risk considers shared attack paths. Judging each item alone is the tempting runner-up because it follows the rating on the report, but it understates the combined risk.

compare.scenario: A configuration change appears on a server with no approved change record. Which response is better?
compare.optionA: Investigate it as a possible unauthorized change before reverting it or processing it after the fact
compare.optionB: Approve it in bulk so that the records match what the monitoring tool reports
compare.why: Unmatched changes are both a compliance gap and a possible incident. Bulk approval is tempting because it clears the alert, but it removes the evidence that change control failed.
